This guide shows how to convert HTML to PDF in C# with PdfPecker, from a one-line conversion to an invoice built from a template and served from ASP.NET Core. PdfPecker is a pure C# library: it does not start Chrome or another browser, needs no native binaries such as wkhtmltopdf, and has no NuGet dependencies, so the same code runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, in Docker and in serverless functions.

Invoice

To: {{WebUtility.HtmlEncode(customer)}}

{{rows}}
ItemQtyAmount

Total: {{total:N2}}

"""; return HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { Title = "Invoice" }); } Table headers repeat on every page when a table runs over a page break, and flexbox, grid and the rest of the CSS PdfPecker supports work in templates as they do in a browser.

Does PdfPecker need Chrome, Puppeteer or wkhtmltopdf? No. It has its own HTML parser, CSS engine, layout engine and PDF writer, written in C#. There is nothing to install on the server besides the .NET runtime. Does it run on Linux, in Docker and in Azure Functions or AWS Lambda? Yes. It is pure managed code, so it runs wherever .NET 8 or later runs, on x64 and ARM64. Does it run JavaScript? No. PdfPecker converts the HTML and CSS you give it, which suits templates you control, such as invoices, reports, payslips and letters. Pages that build themselves with JavaScript need a browser-based converter; Compare lists them. How fast is it? A one-page invoice takes about a millisecond once the process is warm. See Performance for the measurements. Is it free for commercial use? Yes. PdfPecker is open source under the MIT license. Can I also convert Markdown, or make PDF/A? Yes: MarkdownToPdf.Convert takes Markdown (see Markdown), and PdfOptions.Conformance makes PDF/A for archiving (see PDF/A, passwords and watermarks).

PdfOptions controls the page, the document properties and how resources are loaded. Every conversion method takes one; leave it out for A4 pages with the defaults below. var options = new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.Letter.Landscape, // A3, A4 (default), A5, Letter, Legal or new PageSize(w, h) in points Margins = PageMargins.FromMillimeters(20, 15, 20, 15), Scale = 1, // like Chrome's print scale (see its docs to match IronPDF's output) ShrinkToFit = true, // lay out too-wide content wider and draw it smaller, as Chrome prints (default) TruncateBandsToWholePoints = false, // round header/footer height attributes down to whole points, as Chrome does BaseDirectory = "/var/app/templates", // where relative image/stylesheet paths are resolved ResourceResolver = url => myCache.Get(url), // serve http(s) or embedded resources yourself; null = default handling UserStyleSheet = "body { font-size: 10pt }", // extra CSS applied after the document's own FooterText = "Page {page} of {pages}", // also HeaderText Title = "Invoice 42", Author = "Accounts", // document properties (Title defaults to <title>) Keywords = "invoice", Creator = "MyApp", // also Subject, and Producer (default "PdfPecker") CustomProperties = { ["RunId"] = "42" }, // your own properties, in the PDF's document information Bookmarks = true, // PDF bookmarks from h1-h6 (default) FormFields = true, // inputs, selects and textareas become fillable fields (default) Compress = true, // Flate-compress page content (default) AllowFileAccess = false, // true: also read files outside BaseDirectory (trusted HTML only) MaxPages = 1000, // refuse longer documents with PdfLimitException (default 100,000) }; byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, options);

Local images and stylesheets are read only from inside BaseDirectory (the input file's folder for ConvertFile): absolute paths, file: URLs, .. and symbolic links that lead outside it are ignored unless AllowFileAccess = true, and converting a string without a BaseDirectory reads no files at all. For HTML from untrusted users, keep it that way, set a low MaxPages, and pass a cancellation token with a timeout (HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, options, token)): cancelling stops the conversion where it is.

A CSS @page { size: A4 landscape; margin: 15mm } rule overrides the page size and margins unless IgnoreCssPageRules is set. Conversion never makes network requests: http(s) images and stylesheets are only loaded through ResourceResolver. Only signing goes online, and only when asked: a timestamp from TimestampUrl, revocation data with FetchRevocationData, and online revocation checks when verifying.

Custom properties are written to the document information dictionary, where Acrobat shows them under Document Properties > Custom and pdfinfo -custom lists them. For PDF/A they are also written to the XMP metadata (Acrobat's pdfx namespace, with the extension schema PDF/A requires), alongside Keywords, Creator and Producer.

By default every PDF records the time it was made and gets a random file identifier, so two conversions of the same HTML differ. Set CreationDate, or the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH environment variable (seconds since 1970, as used by reproducible builds), and the dates are fixed and the identifier is derived from a hash of the file, so the same input gives a byte-identical PDF. PdfMergeOptions, PdfPagesOptions, PdfStampOptions and PdfFormFillOptions have the same CreationDate. Signed and encrypted output still differs each time, since signing time and encryption keys are part of it. var options = new PdfOptions { CreationDate = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero) };

Errors the library raises itself derive from PdfPeckerException: PdfLimitException (a limit such as MaxPages reached), PdfPasswordException and PdfSignatureException. Unreadable input PDFs throw InvalidDataException, and bad arguments the usual ArgumentExceptions; each method's documentation lists what it throws. Every method that writes a file (ConvertFile, StampFile, SignFile, MergeFiles, ...) writes to a temporary file first and replaces the target only when it succeeds, so a failure leaves an existing file untouched. Methods that read or write PDFs take a CancellationToken and have Stream overloads, and ConvertAsync can write straight to a Stream.

grid-template-columns: subgrid and grid-template-rows: subgrid (CSS Grid Level 2) let a grid item that is itself a grid share its parent's tracks on that axis, so the rows of nested cards or the columns of a form line up across the whole grid. The subgrid's items take part in sizing the parent's tracks, gaps come from the parent unless the subgrid sets its own, and line names come from the parent and from the subgrid's own list (including repeat() and repeat(auto-fill, …)). Subgrids nest, and a subgrid that is not a grid item is laid out as none, as in browsers. Rows paginate as the parent grid's rows do. .plans { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 16px } .plan { display: grid; grid-row: span 3; grid-template-rows: subgrid } /* title, features and price line up */

container-type (inline-size or size), container-name and the container shorthand make an element a query container, and @container rules style its descendants by the container's size: width, height, inline-size, block-size, aspect-ratio and orientation, with min-/max- prefixes or range syntax, combined with and, or and not. A name picks a container (@container sidebar (width < 300px)), and style(--compact: 1) queries a custom property. The cq units are percentages of the nearest container's size. One component can then lay itself out for a narrow sidebar and a wide main column without knowing where it is placed. .card-slot { container: card / inline-size } .card { display: grid; gap: 8px } @container card (width >= 400px) { .card { grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr } } .card h3 { font-size: clamp(14px, 5cqi, 22px) } A document that uses container queries is laid out again until the container sizes settle, which takes about two to four times as long; documents without them are laid out as before.

display: table, inline-table, table-row, table-cell and the other table values work on any element, with the anonymous table, row and cell boxes CSS adds around them, so a lone display: table-cell, a table div with only text and an inline-table lay out as in Chrome; border-spacing starts at 0 except on <table>. Column widths are shared out as Chrome does: columns under a cell that spans several are sized by their own content, a percentage width on a spanning cell is shared by the columns it spans, and percentages that add up to more than 100% are cut down from the last column that has one. A table is never narrower than its columns' narrowest content, so a long word or URL widens it instead of running into the next cell, and never narrower than its caption's longest word. Percentage columns that would squeeze the other columns below their narrowest content give way in proportion, so the table keeps its width, and an image with a percentage width in a cell shrinks with the column instead of widening the table. With border-collapse: collapse, each shared border is drawn once and conflicts are resolved as in CSS 2.1 and Chrome: hidden wins, then the wider border, then the style (double, solid, dashed, dotted, ridge, outset, groove, inset), then cell before row, row group and table. Borders on tr, thead, tbody and tfoot take part, and cells sit inside the border that wins on each side. Backgrounds on thead, tbody, tfoot, col and colgroup are painted in the CSS 2.1 order, under the cells' own. caption-side: bottom, empty-cells: hide and cell min-width and max-width work too; a max-width caps its column even below the text's narrowest width, so a nowrap cell with text-overflow: ellipsis is cut at that width. A position: relative cell holds its absolutely positioned content, which moves with vertical-align and is clipped with the cell, and outlines on cells of a collapsed table are drawn above the table.

display: contents makes no box: the element's children, ::before and ::after included, are laid out as children of its parent, so they become flex items, grid cells, or rows and cells of the table around it, such as a <ul> whose items join a grid or a div that wraps table rows. The element's own border, padding, margin, background, transforms and position do not apply, but inherited properties such as colour and font still reach its children, and counters still count. On replaced elements and form controls (img, svg, input, select, progress and the like) it hides the element, as CSS Display asks, and on the root element it acts as block.

text-wrap: balance evens out the lines of a heading or short paragraph (up to six lines, as in Chrome), and text-wrap: pretty rewraps a paragraph's last four lines so it does not end on a single short word. text-wrap-mode and text-wrap-style are the longhands; stable lays out as auto. Neither applies beside floats, with ::first-line, word-break: break-all or line-break: anywhere, or on pages of different widths. h1, h2 { text-wrap: balance } p { text-wrap: pretty } With text-align: justify, text-justify: auto spreads the free space at spaces and, as Chrome does, between Chinese and Japanese characters and CJK punctuation (Korean Hangul only at spaces). inter-word uses only spaces, inter-character (or distribute) every character, as Firefox does, and none leaves lines unjustified. No-break spaces stretch like spaces. Right-to-left and bidirectional lines are justified at spaces only.

writing-mode: vertical-rl, vertical-lr, sideways-rl and sideways-lr on blocks, inline-blocks, flex items and table cells turn the box's text a quarter turn, as Chrome draws Latin text in those modes: column headers in narrow table cells, labels along the side of a card, and spine text. See Limitations for what is not done yet, such as upright CJK. <th style="writing-mode: sideways-lr">Quarter 1</th> <!-- reads from bottom to top -->

shape-outside makes the text beside a float wrap round a shape instead of the float's rectangle, as in Chrome: circle(), ellipse(), inset() (with round corners), polygon() and path(), optionally with a reference box (margin-box, the default, border-box, padding-box, content-box); a box keyword on its own follows the float's border-radius. Images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP) and gradients work too: pixels more opaque than shape-image-threshold (0 to 1, default 0) count as the shape, so text follows the outline of a cut-out photo. shape-margin grows the shape outwards. Lines beside a shape step down a pixel at a time until they fit, as in Chrome. .portrait { float: left; width: 160px; shape-outside: circle(50%); shape-margin: 12px; border-radius: 50% } .logo { float: right; shape-outside: url(logo.png); shape-image-threshold: 0.3 }

initial-letter on ::first-letter makes a drop cap, as in Chrome. initial-letter: 3 (or 3 drop) is three lines tall and sits on the third line's baseline, 3 raise stands on the first line, and 3 2 sinks two lines; sizes such as 2.5 work too. The letter's font size is chosen so its cap height spans the lines, the lines beside it flow round it like a float, and padding, borders, backgrounds and colours on the letter apply. article > p:first-of-type::first-letter { initial-letter: 3; color: #8b1e3f; margin-right: 6px }

mask-image, mask-size, mask-position, mask-repeat, mask-origin, mask-clip, mask-mode, mask-composite and the mask shorthand work on HTML elements, and so do the -webkit-mask spellings. Mask layers take the same images as backgrounds (gradients, PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, SVG files and data: URIs) and are sized and tiled the same way; url(#id) points at an SVG <mask> in the document. A mask is a PDF soft mask, so masked text stays text: selectable, searchable and tagged. If no mask layer loads, the element is drawn unmasked, as in Chrome. backdrop-filter (and -webkit-backdrop-filter) takes every filter function. What is behind the box is rendered at 144 dpi, filtered and drawn under the box, clipped to its border box and rounded corners; the box's own content stays vector. Chrome's own print to PDF leaves out backdrop-filter and mask-composite; PdfPecker draws them as Chrome shows them on screen. .fade { mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, black 60%, transparent) } .glass { background: rgb(255 255 255 / 40%); backdrop-filter: blur(8px) saturate(1.4) }

translate3d(), translateZ(), scale3d(), scaleZ(), rotateX(), rotateY(), rotate3d(), matrix3d(), perspective(), the perspective and perspective-origin properties, and the translate, scale and rotate properties with a z value or an axis are accepted. A PDF page has only flat (affine) transforms, so a 3D transform is drawn flat: rotateY(60deg) makes a box half as wide, and with a perspective the box gets the scale and shear the projection has at its centre, so it stays a rectangle or parallelogram where Chrome draws a trapezoid. A box turned edge-on or away from the viewer is not drawn. transform-style and backface-visibility are accepted and, as in Chrome's print output, both faces of a flip card are drawn.

h: Scale content to fit a box
x:
-pdfpecker-scale-to-fit: shrink on a box with a height or max-height draws its content smaller until it fits the box, for labels, name badges and certificates that have a fixed space for text of any length. The text reflows wider into fewer lines before it gets smaller, and the box's own border and background keep their size. Content that already fits is not changed, and table cells with a height scale their content too. A scaled box is drawn whole, so like a box with break-inside: avoid it moves to the next page rather than across a page break. Scaled boxes nest at most two levels deep.
Dr. Maximiliane Alexandra von Rosenberg-Hohenstein

Lines, images and table rows are never cut in half at a page boundary; table header rows repeat at the top and <tfoot> rows at the bottom of every page a table spans, as in Chrome; backgrounds and borders continue across pages. Flex lines move to the next page as a whole when they don't fit. A grid row breaks across the page boundary where it starts, as in Chrome, and moves whole only when one of its items cannot break (a line of text, an image, or a box with break-inside: avoid). A table inside a flex or grid item breaks across pages like any other table, with its header repeated, and the line or row grows to match. A paragraph that splits leaves at least orphans lines (default 2) at the bottom of a page and carries at least widows lines (default 2) to the next. Headings keep with the content that follows them (break-after: avoid in the default styles), and break-before/break-after: avoid does the same for any block. break-inside: avoid keeps a block or a whole table on one page when it fits. As in Chrome, a margin that runs past the end of a page is dropped rather than carried to the next one (except after a forced break), and a box's top and bottom borders and padding stay on the same page as its first and last content. A box shadow paints on the pages its box reaches but never adds a page of its own.

<a href> becomes a clickable link, whether inline or a block (a card wrapped in a link), and stays clickable on both pages when a page break splits it. External URLs open in the viewer's browser and #id links jump to the element. Headings h1-h6 become the PDF's bookmarks, nested by level; set PdfOptions.Bookmarks = false to leave them out.

Inline and as url() backgrounds, including data:image/svg+xml URIs) with path (all commands, arcs included), rect (incl. rounded), circle, ellipse, line, polyline, polygon, text and tspan (x, y, dx, dy, text-anchor, dominant-baseline, direction, registered fonts and right-to-left text), textPath (text along a path, with startOffset and the path's pathLength, as in Chrome), g, use (also of a symbol, gradient or clip path defined in another inline SVG on the page, with the symbol's viewBox fitted into the use size), nested svg, image (raster images and SVG files, with preserveAspectRatio; inside an SVG file only data: URIs load, as in browsers), viewBox, preserveAspectRatio and transform, drawn as vector paths. Strokes can be dashed with stroke-dasharray and stroke-dashoffset, scaled by pathLength. opacity on a g, use or nested svg fades the group as one, so overlapping children do not show through each other, and text-decoration on text and tspan draws underlines, overlines and line-throughs in the text's fill. linearGradient and radialGradient (both units, gradientTransform, spreadMethod, href inheritance, and stop-opacity that is truly transparent) become PDF shadings, and pattern fills and strokes (both units, viewBox, patternTransform, href inheritance) become PDF tiling patterns. clipPath clips the elements that reference it, and mask (luminance or alpha, both units) becomes a PDF soft mask. marker draws arrowheads and dots at the vertices of paths, lines, polylines and polygons (orient incl. auto and auto-start-reverse, markerUnits, viewBox, refX/refY, clipped to the marker unless overflow="visible"). filter is applied in pixels, at 144 dpi, and drawn as an image, with every filter primitive: feGaussianBlur, feOffset, feDropShadow, feFlood, feMerge, feComposite (all operators), feBlend (separable modes), feColorMatrix, feComponentTransfer, feMorphology, feTurbulence, feImage, feTile, feConvolveMatrix, feDisplacementMap, and feDiffuseLighting and feSpecularLighting with distant, point and spot lights and lighting-color, in linearRGB or sRGB. Primitive subregions (x, y, width, height) work as in Chrome. Text under a filter stays selectable and searchable: an invisible copy of it is kept on top of the image. As in browsers, an SVG file is styled only by its own

JPEG (embedded as-is, RGB, grayscale and CMYK), PNG (all colour types and bit depths, transparency, interlacing), GIF (transparency, interlacing), WebP (lossy, lossless and with alpha), BMP (1 to 32 bits, palettes, RLE, bit fields and alpha) and TIFF (uncompressed, LZW, Deflate, PackBits, CCITT G3 and G4, JPEG; strips or tiles, planar, alpha, 16-bit; bilevel images stay 1 bit per pixel), from files, data: URIs or your ResourceResolver. Animated GIF and WebP files show their first frame, as a PDF page is still. SVG files are drawn as vectors (see SVG above). Opaque PNGs are passed through without re-encoding. An image wider than its box overflows it, as in Chrome; an image wider than the page makes the whole page shrink to fit, as Chrome prints it, and is scaled down on its own only past 1.5 times the page width or with ShrinkToFit off. A percentage width, max-width or padding on an image is a share of the containing block, inline images draw their border, padding, background and shadow, and vertical margins on inline images and SVG take room in the line, all as in Chrome. An whose picture is missing (no src, a file or ResourceResolver that finds nothing, or data that cannot be decoded) prints its alt text instead, as Chrome does, in the text style around it plus the image's own border, padding, colour and font; this works for Markdown's ![alt](missing.png) too. Without alt text, or with alt="", a missing image keeps an empty box of the width and height given.

@page rules set the page size, margins and background, and their margin boxes (@top-left, @top-center, @bottom-right and the other thirteen) print headers and footers with counter(page) and counter(pages), chosen per page with :first, :left and :right. Those three can also change the page's size, margins and background: @page :first { margin-top: 70mm } leaves room for a letterhead on page 1 only, and mirrored :left and :right margins give a bound booklet a wider inner margin, and each page is laid out at its own content width. The first page is a right page; in a right-to-left document (dir="rtl" on <html>) it is a left page, and PDF viewers are told the pages run right to left. On top of that: Named pages: page: wide puts an element on pages styled by @page wide { ... }, with their own size, orientation, margins, background and margin boxes. Content on another named page starts a new page, so a landscape table or a full-bleed cover can sit between portrait pages. Running headers: string-set copies text from the document (content(), attr(), strings and counters) into a named string, and string(name) shows it in a margin box: the chapter title in the page header, say. As in the spec, string(name, first | start | last | first-except) picks which value a page shows. Tables of contents: target-counter(attr(href), page) shows the page number of the element a link points to, and leader(dotted) (or solid, space, or a string) fills the space before it. target-text() shows the linked element's text. The document is laid out again with the numbers it finds, so they are always right. @page { size: A4; margin: 20mm; @top-center { content: string(chapter) } @bottom-right { content: "Page " counter(page) " of " counter(pages) } } @page cover { margin: 0; background: #1d3557; @top-center { content: none } @bottom-right { content: none } } @page wide { size: A4 landscape } .cover { page: cover } .wide-table { page: wide } h2 { string-set: chapter content(); break-before: page } nav a::after { content: leader(dotted) target-counter(attr(href), page) } Chrome supports named pages and margin boxes, but not running strings, target-counter() or leader().

float: footnote moves an element to the footnote area at the bottom of the page its call is on, as in CSS Generated Content for Paged Media. The footnote counter numbers them; ::footnote-call styles the number in the text (a superscript by default) and ::footnote-marker the number before the note. @page { counter-reset: footnote } restarts the numbering on every page, and @footnote inside @page styles the area with margins, padding, borders, a background and max-height. footnote-display: inline runs short notes together on one line, and footnote-policy: line moves the line with the call to the next page when its note does not fit. A long note continues on the next page. Each call links to its note, and tagged PDFs mark the notes as Note (PDF/UA-1) or FENote (PDF/UA-2). .note { float: footnote; font-size: 8pt } .note::footnote-call { content: "[" counter(footnote) "]"; vertical-align: baseline } @page { @footnote { border-top: 0.5pt solid #999; padding-top: 4pt; margin-top: 8pt } }

When content sticks out past the right edge of the page area, Chrome prints the page laid out as much wider as the content reaches and drawn smaller, and PdfPecker does the same. A box or image wider than the page, a long word or white-space: nowrap text, a Bootstrap .row without a .container (its negative margin), a relative offset, a translateX() or an absolutely positioned box can each widen the layout, by at most 1.5 times (drawn at 67%), on top of Scale. The paper keeps its size and the margins keep theirs. As in Chrome, overflow to the left, content inside an overflow: hidden or clip box (other than html and body) and position: fixed boxes do not count. Set ShrinkToFit = false to lay the document out at the page width as before 1.18.0, with the overflow running into the margin; an image wider than the page is then scaled down on its own. var pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { ShrinkToFit = false });

Markdown goes to PDF through the same engine as HTML: it is turned into HTML with a GitHub-like stylesheet first, so everything on HTML and CSS support applies to it. You can also stop at the HTML. // Markdown to PDF, styled like a GitHub README byte[] pdf = MarkdownToPdf.Convert(File.ReadAllText("README.md")); // File to file; relative image paths resolve against the Markdown file's folder MarkdownToPdf.ConvertFile("README.md", "README.pdf", new PdfOptions { FooterText = "Page {page} of {pages}" }); // Markdown to HTML: a body fragment, or a complete page with the stylesheet string fragment = MarkdownToHtml.Convert("# Hello *World*"); //

string page = MarkdownToHtml.ConvertDocument(markdown); MarkdownToHtml.ConvertFile("README.md", "README.html"); MarkdownOptions switches the GitHub extensions off for strict CommonMark (GitHubExtensions = false), drops heading ids (HeadingIds = false), shows raw HTML as text (AllowRawHtml = false), replaces the stylesheet (StyleSheet, see MarkdownToHtml.DefaultStyleSheet) or sets the title (default: the front matter's title, else the first heading). MarkdownToPdf takes PdfOptions and MarkdownOptions side by side.

CommonMark 0.31 (651 of the 652 spec examples pass; the one miss is an exotic HTML5 entity name) plus the GitHub Flavored Markdown extensions: tables with column alignment, ~~strikethrough~~, task list items (- [x]) and bare www./https:///e-mail autolinks, along with footnotes, definition lists and YAML front matter (see below). Headings get GitHub-style ids, so [see below](#heading-text) links work in the PDF too. The parser runs in linear time on hostile input (deep nesting, unclosed brackets, long delimiter runs). See Limitations for what is not supported.

h: Footnotes, definition lists and front matter
x: Footnotes use GitHub's syntax and are numbered in the order they are first referenced. MarkdownToPdf puts each note at the bottom of the page that references it, with the CSS float: footnote engine, so this also works with your own StyleSheet; MarkdownToHtml lists the notes at the end with links back to the text, as GitHub does. PdfPecker has no dependencies.[^bcl] [^bcl]: Only the .NET base class library. A definition list is a term on its own line followed by one or more lines starting with : , as in PHP Markdown Extra and markdown-it. Front matter between --- lines at the very start of the file is not shown; its title becomes the document's title (the PDF title, and <title> in HTML) unless MarkdownOptions.Title is set. --- title: Release notes --- Subset : Only the glyphs a document uses are embedded. All three are GitHub extensions, so GitHubExtensions = false turns them off along with tables and strikethrough.

PdfPecker.Fluent builds PDFs from C# code instead of HTML, in the style of QuestPDF. You describe pages, headers, footers, columns, rows, tables, text, images and barcodes in code; PdfPecker.Fluent writes compact HTML and CSS for them and renders it with PdfPecker. It needs no browser, no native binaries and no package other than PdfPecker. dotnet add package PdfPecker.Fluent It is released together with PdfPecker, always with the same version, and depends on the PdfPecker release of that version. It runs on .NET 8, 9 and 10, and is trimmable and Native AOT compatible. using PdfPecker.Fluent; Document.Create(container => { container.Page(page => { page.Size(PageSizes.A4); page.Margin(2, Unit.Centimetre); page.DefaultTextStyle(x => x.FontSize(11)); page.Header().Text("Hello PdfPecker").FontSize(20).Bold().FontColor(Colors.Blue.Darken2); page.Content().PaddingVertical(1, Unit.Centimetre).Column(column => { column.Spacing(10); column.Item().Text("A paragraph of text."); column.Item().Image(File.ReadAllBytes("logo.png")).FitWidth(); }); page.Footer().AlignCenter().Text(x => { x.Span("Page "); x.CurrentPageNumber(); x.Span(" of "); x.TotalPages(); }); }); }) .GeneratePdf("hello.pdf");

Layout: Column, Row, Table (row and column spans, header and footer rows repeated on every page), padding, borders, corner radius, background, sizes, alignment, page breaks, Layers, Inlined, MultiColumn, EnsureSpace, Decoration, lists and transforms. Text: spans with font, size, weight, colour, decoration, spacing, superscript and subscript, OpenType features, justified text, ClampLines, headings that become bookmarks, links, and page numbers in the header and footer. Images and graphics: PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, TIFF, GIF and SVG images, lines, and QR, EPC payment QR, Code 128 and EAN-13 barcodes. Accessibility: QuestPDF's Semantic* calls write the HTML PdfPecker tags a PDF/UA document from. Everything else in PdfPecker through PdfOptions: PDF/A, PDF/UA, signatures, passwords, watermarks, e-invoices, attachments and fonts. Output: GeneratePdf (bytes, file or stream), GeneratePdfAsync, GenerateImages and GenerateHtml, which shows the HTML PdfPecker renders. Text, links, colours and names you pass are encoded, so caller data never turns into markup. Html() and Css() are the exception: they insert trusted HTML and CSS as they are, for anything the fluent calls don't cover yet, so never pass user input to them.

Most QuestPDF code ports by changing the using lines: Document.Create, Page, Header, Content, Footer, Column, Row, Table, Text, Padding, Border, Background, Align*, Width, Height and GeneratePdf have the same names. Not available yet: Dynamic, Canvas, StopPaging, ShowOnce, SkipOnce, RepeatContent, ScaleToFit and some section page numbers. The package's README lists every difference. The fluent layer adds well under a millisecond to a typical document. On the same invoice, built call for call, it is about four times as fast as QuestPDF 2026.9.1, as measured in the PdfPecker.Benchmarks repository.

ImageToPdf puts images into a PDF, one per page, such as scanned receipts, photos or drawings for an archive. It reads PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP and TIFF (the first frame of an animated GIF or a multi-page TIFF). // Each page the size of its image byte[] pdf = ImageToPdf.Convert(new[] { File.ReadAllBytes("scan-1.jpg"), File.ReadAllBytes("scan-2.png") }); // Files in, file out ImageToPdf.ConvertFiles(new[] { "receipt-1.jpg", "receipt-2.jpg" }, "receipts.pdf"); // A4 pages with margins, each image centred and scaled down to fit, as PDF/A for archiving byte[] archive = ImageToPdf.Convert(scans, new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.A4, Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA2b, Title = "Receipts 2026" }, new ImageToPdfOptions { FitPageToImage = false });

By default every page is exactly the size of its image, with no margins. ImageToPdfOptions.Dpi (default 96, one image pixel per CSS pixel) sets the printed size: a scan 2,480 pixels wide at 300 dpi becomes an A4-wide page. With FitPageToImage = false every page has the PdfOptions page size and margins. Each image is centred, and scaled down to fit when it is larger than the space inside the margins; smaller images keep their size.
The PdfOptions work as for HTML to PDF: metadata, PDF/A, passwords and watermarks, and a fixed CreationDate for byte-identical output. JPEG images are embedded as they are, without re-encoding.

An empty list or more than ImageToPdf.MaxImages (10,000) images throws ArgumentException, as does a Dpi that is not a positive number. An image that is not in a supported format or is damaged throws InvalidDataException naming its position ("Image 2 ..."), and more images than PdfOptions.MaxPages throws PdfLimitException. An overload takes a cancellation token.

Documents can bring their own fonts with @font-face (files, data: URIs or ResourceResolver URLs; local() refers to registered fonts): @font-face { font-family: Brand; src: url(fonts/brand.woff2) format("woff2"); font-weight: 400; } @font-face { font-family: Brand; src: url(fonts/brand-bold.ttf); font-weight: 700; unicode-range: U+0000-024F; } A FontCollection can be shared between options and parallel conversions. Formats: .ttf, .otf, .ttc collections, WOFF and WOFF2 (including WOFF2 collections; decoded with .NET's built-in Brotli). Fonts are matched like browsers do: by family, then style, then the nearest weight; a missing bold or italic face is synthesized. With the font-stretch descriptor (a keyword, a percentage or a range such as 75% 100%), faces of one family are matched by width first, as in browsers, and a variable font's wdth axis is kept within the declared range. font-display is accepted and ignored, since nothing loads progressively. A character that the chosen font lacks is drawn with the next font in the font-family list that has it, then the standard font, then any other registered font.

Variable fonts (one file with a weight, width, slant or other axis, with TrueType or CFF2 outlines) work with the usual CSS properties. PdfPecker builds a static instance of the font, with its kerning, for each combination a document uses and embeds a subset of it, so bold text uses the font's real bold rather than a synthesized one: @font-face { font-family: Inter; src: url(fonts/InterVariable.ttf); } /* covers all of the font's weights */ h1 { font-family: Inter; font-weight: 750; } .narrow { font-stretch: 75%; } /* the wdth axis */ em { font-style: italic; } /* the ital axis, or slnt */ .custom { font-variation-settings: "wght" 650, "GRAD" 50; } /* any axis, overrides the rest */ A variable @font-face without font-weight covers the font's whole weight range, and so does a variable font added through options.Fonts. A face declared with a single weight (font-weight: 400) stays at that weight, and bold is synthesized as for any other font. The optical size axis (opsz) follows the font size unless font-optical-sizing: none is set. CFF2 fonts are embedded as ordinary CFF fonts, since few PDF readers can draw CFF2.

font-variant-numeric and font-feature-settings turn on a font's optional glyphs, as in a browser. Tabular figures line up amounts in a column: td.amount { font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; } /* every digit the same width */ .oldstyle { font-variant-numeric: oldstyle-nums slashed-zero; } .alt { font-feature-settings: "ss01", "salt" 2; } /* stylistic set 1, the second alternate */ Features that swap one glyph for another (tnum, pnum, lnum, onum, zero, ss01 to ss20, salt, case and the like) are applied; the font must have them. Fractions with font-variant-numeric: diagonal-fractions or font-feature-settings: "frac" are formed as Chrome forms them: the font's contextual rules turn 1/2 and 11/16 into fractions and leave a/b as it is, and tabular-nums used with them does not widen the fraction's digits. Text copied from the PDF keeps the original characters.

font-kerning: none turns kerning off (so does font-feature-settings: "kern" 0), for the standard fonts too. font-synthesis: none (or the longhands font-synthesis-weight, -style and -small-caps) stops the made-up bold and italic for an @font-face family that has only a regular face, as in Chrome. font-size-adjust (a number, from-font, or ex-height, cap-height, ch-width, ic-width or ic-height with a number) draws text in the size that gives the first font of the family that proportion, so a fallback font with small letters does not look smaller; em units and line-height numbers keep the computed size. font-variant-position: sub | super uses the font's own subs and sups glyphs; a font without them is unchanged, as in Chrome. font-variant-east-asian (jis78 to jis04, simplified, traditional, full-width, proportional-width, ruby) picks the font's alternate CJK glyphs. font-variant-caps: small-caps and all-small-caps use the font's own smcp and c2sc glyphs when it has them, and otherwise scaled capitals, unless font-synthesis turns that off.

Text without a registered font uses the standard PDF fonts (Helvetica, Times, Courier), which viewers supply themselves, so files stay small but are limited to Western European characters. Set EmbedStandardFonts = true to embed the bundled Liberation fonts in their place instead: they have the same widths, so the layout does not change, the text looks the same in every viewer, and any character they cover (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, ...) works. PDF/A always does this. It adds a subset of each font used to the file (typically 10-25 KB per font).

A family that no font provides falls back silently, like in a browser. To notice, set MissingFont: it is called once per conversion for each family that had to be substituted, and throwing from it fails the conversion. To use the fonts installed on the machine for families you have not registered, set UseSystemFonts = true (off by default, so the output does not depend on the machine): options.MissingFont = family => logger.LogWarning("Font {Family} is not available", family); options.UseSystemFonts = true; // looks in C:\Windows\Fonts, /Library/Fonts, /usr/share/fonts, ... A character that none of the document's fonts has falls back to fonts built into PdfPecker, as a browser falls back to the system's fonts: Central European, Greek and Cyrillic letters are drawn with the bundled Liberation font that matches the standard font (so they no longer turn into ? when the standard fonts are not embedded), and arrows, check marks, stars, dingbats, math and technical symbols, enclosed numbers, box drawing and geometric shapes with PdfPecker Symbols, a 1,424-character subset of DejaVu Sans. Only the characters used are embedded, and a document that needs no fallback is written exactly as before. A character that no font has, the built-in ones included, is drawn as an empty box (blank space in PDF/A). MissingCharacter is called once for each such character before anything is written, so a test can make sure a template's fonts cover its data: options.MissingCharacter = ch => throw new InvalidOperationException($"No font has U+{char.ConvertToUtf32(ch, 0):X4}");

Registered and @font-face TrueType/OpenType fonts are embedded as subsets (Type0/CIDFontType2 for TrueType outlines, CIDFontType0 with an OpenType program for CFF outlines) with a ToUnicode map, so text can be searched and copied. Without them, the PDF standard fonts are used: font-family maps to Helvetica (sans-serif, Arial, Verdana, ...), Times (serif, Georgia, ...) or Courier (monospace, Consolas, ...), each in regular, bold, italic and bold italic. With EmbedStandardFonts or PDF/A, these are replaced by embedded subsets of the bundled, metric-compatible Liberation Sans, Serif and Mono.

Chinese and Japanese are written without spaces, so a line may break between almost any two characters. PdfPecker finds those breaks with the Unicode Line Breaking Algorithm (UAX #14) and the Japanese kinsoku rules, as browsers do: a line never starts with closing punctuation such as 。, 、 or 」, or with an iteration mark such as 々, and never ends with an opening bracket or quotation mark. Nothing is drawn at these breaks, and Latin words, numbers and emoji sequences inside the text stay whole. Text in other scripts breaks at spaces and hyphens, as before. Fullwidth CJK punctuation such as （, 」 and 。 is drawn with blank space on one side. text-spacing-trim trims that blank half where it would look too wide, as Chrome does. The default, normal, trims it where two punctuation marks meet (）。, ：「, 。」), and a closing bracket or quote at the end of a line also loses its blank half when that lets it fit. space-first also trims the opening bracket that starts each wrapped line, trim-start the one that starts any line, and space-all turns trimming off and keeps the spacing of PdfPecker 1.16 and earlier. Trimming needs a font with the OpenType halt feature, which Noto Sans CJK, Source Han and most Chinese and Japanese fonts have. The font decides whether dots, colons and quotes count as opening or closing (Simplified Chinese fonts draw ，。： on the left, Traditional Chinese ones centre them), and font-feature-settings that set punctuation widths themselves (palt, halt, pwid and the like) turn trimming off, as in Chrome.

hyphens: auto hyphenates words with the TeX hyphenation patterns (Liang's algorithm) of the text's language: the nearest lang attribute, else PdfOptions.Language. As in Chrome, a word is hyphenated only where it does not fit on its line, and a hyphen (or the hyphenate-character) is shown at the break. Words shorter than five letters, words with digits or other non-letters inside, URLs and e-mail addresses, and capitalized English words are not hyphenated, and a word with ­ breaks only there. French and Italian also hyphenate words with an elided article or pronoun, such as l'ordinateur in French or l'informazione in Italian, with a straight or typographic apostrophe. hyphenate-limit-chars sets the shortest word that is hyphenated and the fewest letters before and after a hyphen: up to three values, each auto or a whole number, such as hyphenate-limit-chars: 8 3 3. One value sets only the word length; with two, the letters after a hyphen are the same as before it. It is inherited, so it can be set on the whole document or on a single element. auto keeps the defaults above: words of at least five letters, and the patterns' own minimums around a hyphen (two letters before and three after in English, as in Chrome). Larger values make hyphenation more selective; smaller values do not go below the patterns' own minimums, as in Chrome. For archiving, set Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA2b (or another level below): the PDF gets XMP metadata, an sRGB output intent and a file ID, and CMYK JPEGs are converted to RGB. All fonts are embedded: text without a registered font uses the bundled Liberation fonts (see Fonts). PDF/A does not allow encryption, so combining Conformance with Security throws an ArgumentException. var options = new PdfOptions { Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA4 }; Level Standard File Use it for PdfA2b, PdfA3b ISO 19005-2/-3, level B PDF 1.7 the usual archive format; part 3 also allows attachments (e-invoices) PdfA2u, PdfA3u ISO 19005-2/-3, level U PDF 1.7 as level B, plus a Unicode mapping for every character, so text can be searched and copied PdfA4 ISO 19005-4:2020 PDF 2.0 the current part; identified in the XMP only (pdfaid:rev 2020, no conformance letter), no document information dictionary PdfA4f ISO 19005-4:2020, with files PDF 2.0 PDF/A-4 with attachments: only with EInvoice (it throws without one) Every font is embedded with a ToUnicode map, and a character no font has is left out as blank space rather than drawn as .notdef (in SVG text too), so levels U cost nothing over B. A PDF 2.0 file keeps the title, author, keywords and custom properties in its XMP metadata, since PDF 2.0 deprecates the information dictionary. Every level, on its own and with PDF/UA, passes veraPDF 1.28 (flavours 2b, 2u, 3b, 3u, 4 and 4f) on documents with text, tables, lists, images, links, form fields, SVG and Markdown. AES-256 keys come from a password hash that is slow on purpose, which adds about 3 ms to a conversion.

To add, change or remove the password of a PDF you already have (from any producer, not only PdfPecker), use PdfProtector: // Encrypt any PDF with AES-256 byte[] locked = PdfProtector.Encrypt(pdf, new PdfSecurity { UserPassword = "1234", Permissions = PdfPermissions.Print }); // Change the passwords or permissions of an encrypted PDF (give its current user or owner password) byte[] relocked = PdfProtector.Encrypt(locked, new PdfSecurity { UserPassword = "5678" }, password: "1234"); // Remove the encryption, and with it the permission restrictions byte[] open = PdfProtector.Decrypt(locked, "1234"); // Stream overloads, and a check PdfProtector.Encrypt(inputStream, outputStream, security); bool encrypted = PdfProtector.IsEncrypted(pdf); Encrypted inputs can use RC4 (40 to 128 bit), AES-128 or AES-256; the output of Encrypt is always AES-256. Like other PDF tools, PdfProtector accepts the user password as well as the owner password (or none, for a file that only restricts permissions), so anyone who can open a document can also lift its permissions. A wrong password throws PdfPasswordException. The document is rewritten as a whole and keeps its pages, bookmarks, links, form fields and values, tags, metadata, page labels and attachments; earlier revisions from incremental updates are dropped. Signed PDFs are refused with an ArgumentException (rewriting them would break the signatures; sign after encrypting instead), as is encrypting a PDF/A file, or a PDF/UA file without PdfPermissions.ExtractForAccessibility. Decrypt returns a PDF that is not encrypted unchanged. Watermark applies while converting HTML; to stamp a PDF you already have, see Stamping PDFs.

var options = new PdfOptions { Accessibility = PdfAccessibility.PdfUA1, // or PdfUA2, or Tagged: the same structure without the PDF/UA claim Language = "da", // default: <html lang="...">; for PDF/UA without either, "en" Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA2b, // optional: PDF/UA-1 combines with PDF/A-2 and 3, PDF/UA-2 with PDF/A-4 };

Tagged gives the PDF a structure tree built from the HTML, so screen readers, reflow and text extraction follow the document rather than the page layout: headings (H1 to H6), paragraphs, lists with their labels, tables with header scopes and spans, figures with their alt text, links (tied to their clickable areas), block quotes, code and sections, all in document order, with lang attributes as the language of the element. Text outside a paragraph (straight in a div, say) gets one. Backgrounds, borders, running headers and footers, HeaderText/FooterText, watermarks, repeated table headers, fixed boxes and decorative images are artifacts that assistive technology skips.

PdfUA1 adds what ISO 14289-1 asks beyond the tags: every font embedded (the bundled Liberation fonts stand in for the standard ones), the title shown in the viewer's title bar and the PDF/UA identification in the XMP metadata. The output passes veraPDF's PDF/UA-1 checks, on its own and together with PDF/A-2b or PDF/A-3b (e-invoices included). It needs a title: Title, the <title> element or else the first heading; without one, conversion throws ArgumentException, as it does when Security leaves out PdfPermissions.ExtractForAccessibility.

PdfUA2 (ISO 14289-2:2024) is the PDF 2.0 successor: the file is written as PDF 2.0, its tags are in the PDF 2.0 structure namespace (block quotes, quotes and code, which PDF 2.0 dropped, keep their PDF 1.7 type and are role mapped to Div and Span), links and bookmarks go to structure destinations (the element they point at, not only its page), lists state their numbering and form fields describe themselves, and the XMP says pdfuaid:part 2 with pdfuaid:rev 2024. It has the same title and language requirements as PdfUA1 and passes veraPDF's PDF/UA-2 checks, on its own and with PdfA4. PDF/UA-1 and PDF/A-2 and 3 are based on PDF 1.7, PDF/UA-2 and PDF/A-4 on PDF 2.0, so PdfUA2 with PdfA2b (or any PDF/A-2 or 3 level) and PdfUA1 with PdfA4 throw ArgumentException.

What the tags can't fix is up to the HTML: give images an alt (an image without alt, aria-label or title, or an <svg> without a <title>, counts as decorative), use real headings, lists and th cells, and mark purely visual content aria-hidden="true". Heading levels that skip one (h1 then h3) are tagged one level below the previous heading, as PDF/UA does not allow gaps.
