Forms work with Security (the values are encrypted with the rest), Conformance (veraPDF passes the fields as PDF/A-2b and 3b), Accessibility (each widget sits in a Form element described by its label, title or name, and veraPDF passes PDF/UA-1), Signature (the signature field joins the form) and PdfMerger (repeated names are renamed).

PdfForm reads, fills and flattens the form fields of any PDF, not only those PdfPecker made, such as a government form or a contract template from another tool: // The fields, by fully qualified name ("address.city" for a nested one). foreach (PdfFormField field in PdfForm.GetFields(pdf)) Console.WriteLine($"{field.Name} ({field.Type}) = {field.Value}, choices: {string.Join(", ", field.Options)}"); var values = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["name"] = "Jane Doe", ["address.city"] = "Copenhagen", ["newsletter"] = "true", // a check box: its on state, or true/yes/on/1; Off/false/no/0/"" clears it ["size"] = "M", // a radio button group: the state name of one button ["country"] = "dk", // a combo box or list box: a choice's value or its text }; byte[] filled = PdfForm.Fill(pdf, values); // Fill and flatten in one go, so the values can no longer be changed; or flatten a PDF as it is. byte[] final = PdfForm.Fill(pdf, values, new PdfFormFillOptions { Flatten = true }); byte[] flat = PdfForm.Flatten(filled); PdfForm.FillFile("application.pdf", "application-filled.pdf", values); PdfFormField gives each field's Type (Text, CheckBox, RadioButton, ComboBox, ListBox, PushButton or Signature), its Value (and Values for a list box with several choices), the Options it accepts, its flags (ReadOnly, Required, Multiline, MaxLength, ...), its tooltip and the page it is on. A name that is no field, a choice the field does not have, or text longer than MaxLength throws ArgumentException; set IgnoreUnknownFields to skip names the PDF does not have. Push buttons and signature fields cannot be filled (sign the latter with PdfSigner). Every filled field gets a new appearance in the field's own font, size, colour and alignment, with automatic font size, multi-line text and comb fields laid out, and the box and background of its old appearance kept, so the values show in every viewer and in PdfToImage. When the field's font cannot show a value, a subset of PdfFormFillOptions.Font (by default the bundled Liberation Sans, which covers Latin, Greek and Cyrillic) is embedded for it. XFA form data, which would override the filled fields in some viewers, is removed. A signed or encrypted PDF is filled with an incremental update: the original bytes stay as they were, so the signatures stay valid (when their permissions allow form filling) and the encryption is kept; pass the password in PdfFormFillOptions.Password. Other PDFs are written out in full, without the old values in earlier revisions. Flattening draws each field into its page and removes it, keeping links, comments and other annotations; it changes the pages, so a signed PDF is refused with InvalidOperationException.

Sign the PDF with a certificate (a .pfx file or one from the certificate store). Adobe Reader then shows who signed it and whether the file was changed afterwards. The key can also stay in an HSM, smart card or cloud key vault (external signers), and the signatures of any PDF can be verified and made verifiable for years. var cert = X509CertificateLoader.LoadPkcs12FromFile("signer.pfx", "pfx-password"); var options = new PdfOptions { Signature = new PdfSignatureOptions(cert) { Reason = "Approved", Location = "Copenhagen", // Optional: a visible box (points from the top-left corner; Page = -1 is the last page). Appearance = new PdfSignatureAppearance { Page = -1, X = 340, Y = 720, Width = 220, Height = 70 }, // Optional: a trusted RFC 3161 timestamp (PAdES B-T). The only option that uses the network. TimestampUrl = "http://timestamp.digicert.com", }, }; // Or sign any existing PDF; earlier signatures stay valid. byte[] signed = PdfSigner.Sign(File.ReadAllBytes("in.pdf"), new PdfSignatureOptions(cert)); // A contract template with empty signature fields: sign into one by name, at its place on the page. byte[] countersigned = PdfSigner.Sign(contract, new PdfSignatureOptions(cert) { FieldName = "Buyer" });

When FieldName names an empty signature field the PDF already has ("Parties.Buyer" for a nested one), the signature goes into it and the box fills the field's rectangle; signing a field of another type or one that is already signed throws PdfSignatureException. Any other name adds a new field.

Signatures are PAdES baseline (ETSI.CAdES.detached) by default, or classic adbe.pkcs7.detached with Format = PdfSignatureFormat.Pkcs7Detached; RSA and ECDSA keys with SHA-256/384/512. The signature is appended as an incremental update, and it works together with Security (encrypted files) and Conformance (PDF/A: the visible box is drawn as outlines, so it needs no unembedded font). The CMS structure is built with .NET's own System.Formats.Asn1 and System.Security.Cryptography; no extra package is needed. Signing adds a few milliseconds (the RSA or ECDSA operation and re-reading the file); conversions without a signature are unaffected.

h: External signers: HSMs, smart cards and key vaults
x: When the private key cannot leave its hardware security module, smart card, PKCS#11 token or cloud key vault, pass a PdfExternalSigner with the certificate. PdfPecker builds the PDF and the CMS structure, and asks your callback only for the raw signature value. The certificate needs only its public part. The callback gets a PdfSignatureRequest with Digest for "sign hash" APIs (Azure Key Vault SignAsync, AWS KMS Sign with MessageType.DIGEST, RSA.SignHash) and Data for APIs that hash themselves; both give the same signature. // The certificate without its private key; the key stays in Azure Key Vault. var cert = X509CertificateLoader.LoadCertificateFromFile("signer.cer"); var keyVault = new CryptographyClient(keyId, new DefaultAzureCredential()); var signer = new PdfExternalSigner(PdfSignatureAlgorithm.RsaPkcs1, async (request, ct) => (await keyVault.SignAsync(SignatureAlgorithm.RS256, request.Digest.ToArray(), ct)).Signature); byte[] signed = await PdfSigner.SignAsync(pdf, new PdfSignatureOptions(cert, signer) { Reason = "Approved" }); // A synchronous callback, here with a key .NET can use directly (such as one from a PKCS#11 wrapper). var local = new PdfExternalSigner(PdfSignatureAlgorithm.RsaPss, request => rsa.SignHash(request.Digest.ToArray(), request.HashAlgorithm, RSASignaturePadding.Pss)); byte[] signed2 = PdfSigner.Sign(pdf, new PdfSignatureOptions(cert, local)); PdfSignatureAlgorithm is RsaPkcs1 (RS256 and the like), RsaPss (PS256, with a salt as long as the hash) or Ecdsa (ES256, DER-encoded or raw r||s); the hash is PdfSignatureOptions.HashAlgorithm, SHA-256 by default. The returned signature is checked against the certificate before it goes into the PDF, so a wrong key or padding throws PdfSignatureException instead of producing a broken file. The callback is normally called once per signature (twice in the rare case the signature does not fit the space reserved for it). PdfSigner.SignAsync awaits an asynchronous callback and the timestamp server instead of blocking a thread; PdfSigner.Sign and signing during HtmlToPdf.Convert with PdfOptions.Signature wait for it. Everything else, visible boxes, timestamps and existing fields, works as with a certificate's own key.

PdfSignatureVerifier checks the signatures and document timestamps of any PDF, oldest first, and reports what it finds rather than throwing for a broken signature: foreach (PdfSignatureVerification s in PdfSignatureVerifier.Verify(pdf)) { Console.WriteLine($"{s.FieldName}: signed by {s.SignerName} at {s.TimestampTime ?? s.SigningTime}"); Console.WriteLine($" valid: {s.Valid}, intact: {s.IsIntact}, covers the whole file: {s.CoversWholeDocument}"); foreach (string problem in s.Problems) Console.WriteLine(" " + problem); } // Trust only your own CA instead of the operating system's roots, and check revocation online. var results = PdfSignatureVerifier.VerifyFile("contract.pdf", new PdfSignatureVerificationOptions { TrustedRoots = new X509Certificate2Collection(companyRootCert), RevocationMode = X509RevocationMode.Online, }); IsIntact means the signed bytes are unchanged (DigestMatches), the byte range is well formed (ByteRangeValid), the signature value verifies with the signer's certificate (SignatureValid) and an embedded timestamp, if any, is sound (TimestampValid). Valid adds that the certificate chains to a trusted root (ChainTrusted, with ChainErrors saying why not). Chains are built from the certificates in the signature, the PDF's Document Security Store and ExtraCertificates. Verification is offline by default: RevocationMode is NoCheck unless you set it, and VerificationTime checks the chain at another time. Trusted timestamps The chain is checked at the time of the signature's timestamp only when TimestampTrusted is true: the timestamp authority's certificate chains to the same trusted roots as the signer's and carries the timestamping key usage. Anyone can make a token that states any time, so an untrusted timestamp no longer lets an expired signer certificate pass; the chain is then checked now, and the untrusted timestamp is listed in Problems even when the signature is valid without it. The signing time the signer claims is never used. A signer certificate whose key usage allows neither digital signatures nor non-repudiation is not trusted, and a document timestamp's certificate must carry the timestamping usage. Add your timestamp authority's root to TrustedRoots when you trust only your own CA. A signature followed by later changes stays valid, because that is how a second signature or validation data is added: UpdatesAfterSigning counts the incremental updates after it, and CoversWholeDocument is false. What those updates change is not analysed (see Limitations), so check CoversWholeDocument on the last signature when nothing may follow it. PAdES, adbe.pkcs7.detached, adbe.pkcs7.sha1 and document timestamps (ETSI.RFC3161, IsDocumentTimestamp) are read, from PDFs made by any tool.

A signature can normally be checked only while its certificates are valid and their CA answers. PdfSigner.AddValidationData makes it checkable for years: it adds a Document Security Store with every certificate in the chains of the PDF's signatures and timestamps, and the OCSP responses and CRLs that show none was revoked (PAdES B-LT). With TimestampUrl a document timestamp follows, which seals the signatures and the validation data with a trusted time (PAdES B-LTA). Both are incremental updates, so the signatures stay valid. byte[] signed = PdfSigner.Sign(pdf, new PdfSignatureOptions(cert) { TimestampUrl = "http://timestamp.digicert.com" }); byte[] ltv = PdfSigner.AddValidationData(signed, new PdfLtvOptions { FetchRevocationData = true, // ask each certificate's OCSP responder, else its CRL TimestampUrl = "http://timestamp.digicert.com", // PAdES B-LTA }); // Offline: only the chains, completed with your own certificates and revocation data. byte[] offline = PdfSigner.AddValidationData(signed, new PdfLtvOptions { Certificates = [intermediateCert, rootCert], OcspResponses = [ocspResponseDer], }); Without FetchRevocationData or TimestampUrl nothing goes over the network; OCSP and CRL requests use only the http and https addresses in the certificates, through HttpClient if you set one. Those addresses come from the PDF, so set UrlFilter to keep requests away from internal hosts: it is asked about every URL, redirect targets included, and returning false skips it. var options = new PdfLtvOptions { FetchRevocationData = true, UrlFilter = url => url.Host.EndsWith(".digicert.com", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase), }; Whatever the filter says, one call contacts at most 32 distinct URLs (64 requests), follows at most 3 redirects per CRL download (never from https to http), bounds slow responses and stops fetching after two minutes in total. An HttpClient whose handler follows redirects itself does so without asking the filter. To make the document timestamp itself long-term verifiable, call AddValidationData again later without a TimestampUrl. A PDF without signatures throws PdfSignatureException. Sign and AddValidationData take a CancellationToken, and AddValidationDataAsync awaits the OCSP, CRL and timestamp requests instead of blocking a thread. HtmlToPdf.ConvertAsync signs asynchronously with the caller's token. Cancelling throws OperationCanceledException, and an unreadable PDF throws InvalidDataException.

InvoiceData describes an invoice by the European e-invoicing standard EN 16931: the seller and buyer, the lines, allowances and charges, payment and references. PdfPecker calculates the totals and the VAT breakdown from the lines and writes the invoice as XML, so you do not need a separate e-invoicing library: var invoice = new InvoiceData { Number = "INV-2026-0042", IssueDate = new DateOnly(2026, 10, 13), DueDate = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 12), BuyerReference = "04011000-12345-34", Seller = new InvoiceParty { Name = "Example Seller GmbH", VatId = "DE123456789", Address = new InvoiceAddress { Line1 = "Musterstraße 1", City = "Berlin", PostalCode = "10115", CountryCode = "DE" }, ElectronicAddress = "DE123456789", ElectronicAddressScheme = "9930", }, Buyer = new InvoiceParty { Name = "Example Buyer AG", Address = new InvoiceAddress { Line1 = "Beispielweg 2", City = "München", PostalCode = "80331", CountryCode = "DE" }, ElectronicAddress = "04011000-12345-34", ElectronicAddressScheme = "0204", }, Payment = new InvoicePayment { Iban = "DE02 1203 0000 0000 2020 51", Reference = "INV-2026-0042" }, }; invoice.Lines.Add(new InvoiceLine { Name = "Consulting", Quantity = 10, UnitCode = "HUR", NetPrice = 100, VatRate = 19 }); byte[] facturX = invoice.ToCii(); // Factur-X / ZUGFeRD EN 16931 byte[] xrechnung = invoice.ToCii(EInvoiceProfile.XRechnung); // XRechnung 3.0 CII byte[] peppol = invoice.ToUbl(); // Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 UBL byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(invoiceHtml, new PdfOptions { EInvoice = invoice.ToEInvoice() }); // Factur-X PDF ToCii() writes Factur-X / ZUGFeRD EN 16931 CII, and ToCii(EInvoiceProfile.XRechnung) XRechnung 3.0 CII. ToUbl() writes Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 UBL, an Invoice or, for InvoiceType.CreditNote, a CreditNote; ToUbl(UblFormat.XRechnung) writes XRechnung 3.0 UBL. Attach the PDF with UblInvoice.AttachPdf (see below). Peppol needs real participant IDs as electronic addresses, with an EAS scheme such as 0184, 0088 or 9930; an email address (EM) is not accepted. ToEInvoice() returns a PdfEInvoice for PdfOptions.EInvoice, so one conversion makes the Factur-X PDF. CalculateTotals() returns the InvoiceTotals: line total, allowances, charges, net total, the VAT breakdown, grand total and amount due. Money is rounded to two decimals, half away from zero, as EN 16931 expects. Validate() (with an EInvoiceProfile or a UblFormat) lists the problems with their EN 16931 rule numbers, plus XRechnung's BR-DE and the Peppol rules for those formats, or an empty list. ToCii, ToUbl and ToEInvoice throw ArgumentException with every problem in the message. The checks cover the fields the model has; they do not replace the receiver's own validator. VAT categories are standard (S), zero rated (Z), exempt (E, which needs a reason in VatExemptionReasons), reverse charge (AE), intra-community supply (K), export (G), outside scope (O), and the Canary Islands (L) and Ceuta and Melilla (M) taxes. Reverse charge, intra-community supply, export and outside scope get the standard EU wording and VATEX code when no reason is given. The same invoice always gives the same bytes. Only the EN 16931 and XRechnung profiles are written; MINIMUM, BASIC WL, BASIC and EXTENDED throw. The XML passes the Mustang validator (CII and UBL, with XRechnung) and the Peppol BIS 3.0 schematrons.

InvoiceTemplate turns an InvoiceData into a print-ready A4 invoice, with the Factur-X EN 16931 XML embedded by default (which makes the file PDF/A-3b): byte[] pdf = InvoiceTemplate.ToPdf(invoice, new InvoiceTemplateOptions { Logo = File.ReadAllBytes("logo.png"), AccentColor = "#0b6e4f", Labels = InvoiceLabels.German, }); string html = InvoiceTemplate.ToHtml(invoice); // the HTML, to adapt and convert yourself Option Default What it does Logo null Your logo as PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP or SVG bytes, drawn at most 180 by 64 pixels. LogoUri null The logo as a data URI, or a URL your ResourceResolver loads; used when Logo is null. AccentColor #1f4e79 The colour of the title, headings and table header, as CSS. Labels InvoiceLabels.English The texts, number and date formats: start from English, German or Danish and change any text, the decimal and group separators, the date format and the unit names. Css null Extra CSS after the template's own, to change fonts, spacing or anything else. PaymentQrCode true Prints an EPC payment QR code (GiroCode) next to the payment details for euro invoices paid to an IBAN. EInvoice EInvoiceProfile.En16931 The e-invoice ToPdf embeds: En16931, XRechnung, or null for a plain PDF. PdfOptions null The PDF settings to start from, such as fonts, metadata or a signature. They are copied, not changed; page size and margins come from the template's CSS. Long invoices continue on more pages with the table header repeated. The labels need no CultureInfo, so the template also works in apps that run with invariant globalization.

Pass the invoice's CII XML (from your invoicing system, or from InvoiceData.ToCii()) and PdfPecker attaches it to the PDF, making a Factur-X / ZUGFeRD e-invoice: the pages are the human-readable invoice and the XML is what accounting software reads. var options = new PdfOptions { EInvoice = new PdfEInvoice(File.ReadAllBytes("invoice.xml")), }; File.WriteAllBytes("invoice.pdf", HtmlToPdf.Convert(invoiceHtml, options)); The file is PDF/A-3b, so Conformance is raised to PdfA3b when it is left at None; PdfA3u and PdfA4f (PDF/A-4 with attachments) work too, while the other levels and Security throw. Factur-X and ZUGFeRD specify PDF/A-3, so keep the default unless the receiver asks for PDF/A-4f. The XML is embedded unchanged as factur-x.xml (xrechnung.xml for XRechnung), listed as an associated file, and the XMP metadata gets the Factur-X extension schema with the document type, version and profile. The profile (MINIMUM, BASIC WL, BASIC, EN 16931, EXTENDED or XRECHNUNG) is read from the XML's guideline ID; pass it as the second constructor argument to set it yourself. The relationship to the pages defaults to Data for MINIMUM and BASIC WL and Alternative otherwise; set Relationship to change it. PdfPecker checks that the XML is a well-formed Cross Industry Invoice (UBL is not allowed in Factur-X) but does not validate XML you pass in yourself: make sure the visible pages show the same invoice. XML from InvoiceData is checked before it is written. The output passes the Mustang validator (PDF/A-3b via veraPDF, and the XML's schematron). Other files can be attached next to the invoice with Attachments (see Attachments).

h: Reading the invoice from a received PDF
x: PdfEInvoice.Read gets the XML back out of a Factur-X, ZUGFeRD 2.x or XRechnung PDF, from PdfPecker or any other producer, so the accounting side can read what the pages show: PdfEInvoice? invoice = PdfEInvoice.Read(File.ReadAllBytes("received.pdf")); if (invoice is not null) { File.WriteAllBytes("invoice.xml", invoice.Xml); Console.WriteLine(invoice.Profile); // e.g. En16931 } The invoice is the attachment the XMP metadata names, else one called factur-x.xml, zugferd-invoice.xml or xrechnung.xml, else any other attached Cross Industry Invoice. The XML comes back unchanged with its Profile (from the XML's guideline, else the XMP conformance level) and Relationship; PdfPecker does not validate it. The result is null when the PDF carries no invoice. ZUGFeRD 1.0 uses an older schema and is not found, but PdfAttachments.List still returns its file. Pass password for an encrypted PDF.

h: PDF attachments in UBL e-invoices (Peppol, OIOUBL)
x: Peppol BIS Billing 3.0, OIOUBL, EHF, XRechnung UBL and other UBL e-invoices are XML only: the XML is the invoice, and the PDF travels inside it as an attachment. UblInvoice.AttachPdf adds one to the invoice or credit note your invoicing system made: byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(invoiceHtml); byte[] xml = UblInvoice.AttachPdf(File.ReadAllBytes("invoice.xml"), pdf, "INV-1001.pdf"); The PDF goes in as an AdditionalDocumentReference with EmbeddedDocumentBinaryObject (mimeCode="application/pdf" and the file name), after any attachments already there and where the UBL schema expects it. The rest of the XML, including its indentation, encoding and declaration, is kept as it was. The reference ID defaults to the file name; pass id and description to set them. For OIOUBL 2.1 (UBL 2.0) the description is written as the DocumentType OIOUBL requires, PDF by default. The output passes the UBL schemas, the Peppol BIS 3.0 and EN 16931 schematrons, and the OIOUBL 2.1 schematron. PdfPecker does not validate the rest of an invoice you pass in; to build the UBL itself, use InvoiceData.ToUbl() (see above).

Barcode draws QR codes, EPC payment QR codes, Code 128 and EAN-13 barcodes as SVG markup for your HTML template. The SVG stays vector graphics in the PDF, so the code scans at any print size. Like the rest of PdfPecker it needs no other package. // Inline SVG in the template string qr = Barcode.QrCode("https://example.com/invoice/1042"); string html = $"

Scan to pay online:

{qr}"; // Or as an image, a CSS background or a Markdown image string src = Barcode.ToDataUri(Barcode.Ean13("590123412345")); string img = $""; // Code 128 for order numbers, shipping labels and other ASCII text string label = Barcode.Code128("ORDER-2026-1042", new BarcodeOptions { Height = 40, ShowText = false });

Barcode.QrCode picks the smallest QR code (versions 1 to 40) that holds the text at the chosen error correction. Digits only and upper-case alphanumeric text are packed densely, and anything else is stored as UTF-8, up to 2,953 bytes at the lowest level. BarcodeOptions.ErrorCorrection is Low (about 7 percent of the code may be damaged), Medium (15 percent, the default), Quartile (25 percent) or High (30 percent, for codes printed small or with a logo on top). Text that does not fit throws ArgumentException.

Barcode.EpcQrCode draws the European Payments Council's QR code for a euro credit transfer, also called GiroCode, which banking apps read to fill in the payment. Set Name and Iban on an EpcPayment; the rest is optional. string pay = Barcode.EpcQrCode(new EpcPayment { Name = "Example Ltd", Iban = "DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00", Amount = 129.95m, Text = "Invoice 1042", }); The payment follows guideline EPC069-12 (version 002, UTF-8) and is checked before drawing: the IBAN's check digits, an 8 or 11 character Bic, an Amount from 0.01 to 999,999,999.99 with at most two decimals (or null to let the payer enter it), a four-letter Purpose code, and either a structured creditor Reference (ISO 11649, "RF...") or a Text of up to 140 characters, not both. Information is a note shown to the payer. A field that is missing, too long or invalid throws ArgumentException. The code always uses error correction level M, as the guideline requires. ToPayload() returns the text the code holds.

Barcode.Code128 takes 1 to 1,000 ASCII characters and packs runs of digits two to a symbol. Barcode.Ean13 takes 12 digits and adds the check digit, or 13 digits with a correct check digit, and draws the retail barcode with its guard bars. Both print the text below the bars unless ShowText is false.

BarcodeOptions sets: ModuleSize: the width of the narrowest bar or one QR square in CSS pixels, which sets the SVG's size. The default is 3 for QR codes and 1.5 for barcodes. CSS width on the SVG or image scales it too. Height: the bar height of Code 128 and EAN-13 in CSS pixels; the default is 60 modules. QuietZone: the blank margin scanners need around the code (4 modules for QR, 10 for Code 128, 11 and 7 for EAN-13). On by default; turn it off only when the layout leaves that space. Color and Background: CSS colours, #000 on #fff by default. Set Background to null for none, but keep the code dark on light, since scanners need the contrast.

Any file can travel inside the PDF, listed in the viewer's attachments panel: the source spreadsheet of a report, the data behind a chart, a signed contract. var options = new PdfOptions { Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA3b }; // optional options.Attachments.Add(new PdfAttachment("figures.csv", csvBytes) { Description = "The figures behind the charts", // default: the file name Relationship = PdfAttachmentRelationship.Data, // Source, Data, Alternative, Supplement or Unspecified // MimeType = "text/csv", // default: guessed from the extension // CreationDate = ..., ModDate = ... // default: ModDate is the time of conversion }); options.Attachments.Add(PdfAttachment.FromFile("contract.pdf")); byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, options); // Read them back, or attach files to a PDF made elsewhere. foreach (PdfAttachment a in PdfAttachments.List(pdf)) Console.WriteLine($"{a.FileName}: {a.Data.Length} bytes"); byte[]? csv = PdfAttachments.Extract(pdf, "figures.csv"); byte[] more = PdfAttachments.Add(File.ReadAllBytes("scan.pdf"), new PdfAttachment("notes.txt", notes));

Each file is written with its MIME type, size, dates and MD5 checksum, in the document's embedded-files list sorted by name, and as an associated file (/AF) with its relationship to the pages, as PDF/A-3 requires. File names must be unique (ArgumentException otherwise; an attachment can't take the e-invoice's factur-x.xml). Attachments don't change Conformance: without one the file is a plain PDF, PDF/A-3b, PDF/A-3u and PDF/A-4f allow any attachment, and PDF/A-2b, PDF/A-2u and PDF/A-4, which allow only PDF/A files as attachments, throw ArgumentException rather than produce a file that fails validation. With Security the attachments are encrypted with the rest of the file, and for PDF/UA each one gets the description ISO 14289 asks for. The output passes veraPDF's PDF/A-3b, PDF/A-3u, PDF/A-4f, PDF/UA-1 and PDF/UA-2 checks. PdfAttachments.Add likewise refuses PDF/A-1, PDF/A-2 and PDF/A-4 files, and adds to PDF/A-3 and PDF/A-4f files.

PdfAttachments.Add appends the files as an incremental update, so the original bytes, and any digital signatures over them, stay as they were; an encrypted PDF (pass its password) stays encrypted, a PDF/A-3 file gets the new associated files, and PDF/A-1 and PDF/A-2 files are refused. List and Extract read the embedded-files list and associated files of any PDF, decrypting with the password you pass; files attached to page annotations (the paper-clip icons) are not read.

PdfMerger combines PDFs into one, any PDFs, not only those PdfPecker made: byte[] merged = PdfMerger.Merge(invoicePdf, termsPdf, attachmentPdf); // With passwords for encrypted inputs (by position), and properties for the result. byte[] merged2 = PdfMerger.Merge(new[] { a, b }, new PdfMergeOptions { Passwords = new string?[] { null, "secret" }, Title = "Payslips October", CustomProperties = { ["RunId"] = "42" }, }); PdfMerger.MergeFiles("all.pdf", new[] { "a.pdf", "b.pdf" }); // Streams in and out: inputs are read one at a time and the result is written as it is made. PdfMerger.Merge(new[] { invoiceStream, termsStream }, outputStream); await PdfMerger.MergeAsync(uploads.Select(f => f.OpenReadStream()), response.Body); Tagged inputs stay tagged: their structure trees are joined under one root, so the merged file is still accessible, and when every input is PDF/UA-1 the result says so too (veraPDF passes it). The merged file is PDF 1.7, so PDF/UA-2 inputs stay tagged but the result claims no PDF/UA level. An input in another language than the first keeps its language on its own part of the tree. Untagged inputs merge as before. With streams (and MergeFiles), only one input is held in memory at a time and the merged document goes to the output as each input is done, so memory follows the largest input rather than the whole batch: merging 100 files of 32 MB in total peaks at 14 MB of managed memory, against 105 MB with byte arrays. MergeAsync reads and writes asynchronously, as ASP.NET Core requires for request and response bodies. Input streams are read from their current position and are not disposed; the sequence is enumerated lazily, so an iterator can open each one only when its turn comes. MergeFiles writes to a temporary file and moves it into place, so the output can be one of the inputs and a failed merge leaves no partial file behind.

For PDFs that arrive one at a time from elsewhere, such as downloads read a few at a time, use StreamingPdfMerger. It writes each PDF's pages when it is added and then lets the PDF go, so memory stays at about one input, and between inputs you decide what comes next: skip a missing document, or check that anything was added before answering. The output can be an HTTP response body or a file; it does not need to be seekable. var merger = new StreamingPdfMerger(response.Body, new PdfMergeOptions { Title = "Payslips October" }); foreach (var path in paths) { var pdf = await storage.DownloadAsync(path, ct); if (pdf.Length == 0) continue; // skip a missing document await merger.AddAsync(pdf, ct); } if (merger.InputCount == 0) return Results.NotFound(); await merger.CompleteAsync(ct); // writes the page tree, bookmarks, form and cross-reference table // Or, from an IAsyncEnumerable<byte[]>: int pages = await PdfMerger.MergeAsync(DownloadInOrder(paths), response.Body, cancellationToken: ct); The result is the same as PdfMerger.Merge's, but the output is only a valid PDF once Complete has run. If adding a PDF throws (a damaged or encrypted input, MaxPages reached), what was written cannot be used and the merger refuses further calls. Passwords are matched to inputs in the order they are added. The pages keep their content, fonts, images, links, annotations, layers and fillable form fields, and each input's bookmarks follow each other. A form field named like one in an earlier input is renamed name_2, name_3 and so on, so the copies keep their own values. Document properties come from the first input unless PdfMergeOptions sets them. The result is never encrypted (pass it to PdfProtector.Encrypt to protect it) and has no signatures (merging would break them); PDF/A conformance is not carried over. Page labels are kept (pages of an input without them are numbered as in that input), and attachments too, with one named like an earlier input's listed as name (2).ext. Images, fonts and other resources that are byte-for-byte the same in several inputs, such as a logo on every payslip of a run, are written once. Inputs are handled as untrusted: damaged files are repaired where possible, decoding is limited per input, and MaxPages (default 100,000) caps the result. Inputs without any pages throw InvalidDataException. Merging was tested on PDFs from Chrome (as IronPDF makes them), Ghostscript, LibreOffice, MuPDF, qpdf, ReportLab, pypdf incremental updates, scanners (JPEG, CCITT G4, CMYK, OCR text layers) and damaged files (wrong or missing cross-reference tables, truncated files, junk before the header); every merged page rendered pixel-identical to its original in Poppler. Merging four small documents takes about 1 ms, and 1,000 one-page Chrome payslips about 1 s.

PdfPages works on the pages of any existing PDF. Pages are numbered from 1, and ranges are written like "1-3,5,8-" (pages 1 to 3, 5, and 8 to the end): "3,1,2" reorders, "1,1" repeats, "5-3" runs backwards and "last" is the last page. PdfPageRange.Parse reads a range once for reuse; a page past the end throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException ("Page 9 is out of range: the PDF has 5 pages."). byte[] summary = PdfPages.Extract(report, "1-3,5"); // or new[] { 3, 1, 2 } byte[] withoutCover = PdfPages.Remove(report, "1"); byte[] turned = PdfPages.Rotate(scan, 90, "2,4"); // clockwise; null pages = every page byte[][] parts = PdfPages.Split(report, 10); // 10 pages each byte[][] chapters = PdfPages.Split(report, "1-4", "5-9", "10-"); int pages = PdfPages.Count(report); // Encrypted input, files, streams. byte[] page = PdfPages.Extract(secret, "2", new PdfPagesOptions { Password = "pw", Title = "Page 2" }); PdfPages.ExtractFile("report.pdf", "summary.pdf", "1-3"); PdfPages.SplitFile("report.pdf", 1, n => $"report-{n}.pdf"); // Selected pages of several PDFs merged into one (also StreamingPdfMerger.Add(pdf, pages)). byte[] merged = PdfMerger.Merge(new[] { new PdfMergeInput(invoice, "1"), new PdfMergeInput(terms, "2-") }); For the pages taken, the result keeps their content, links and other annotations, the form fields with a widget on them, the bookmarks that go to them, page labels, the document properties and language. Links and bookmarks to pages left out are dropped (a bookmark with a kept bookmark below it stays, without a destination); links between pages taken go to their new place. A tagged input stays tagged: structure elements are kept when some of their content is on a page taken, so a PDF/UA-1 input gives a PDF/UA-1 result (veraPDF passes extracted, removed and split parts). A page taken more than once is copied with its links, but its form fields stay on the first copy and the later copies are not tagged, so such a result no longer claims PDF/UA. Split parses the PDF once for all parts. As with merging, the result is not encrypted and has no signatures.

PdfStamper puts a page of one PDF on top of the pages of another, such as a "PAID" or "COPY" stamp, or underneath them, such as company letterhead. Any PDF can be stamped, not only those PdfPecker made: // A one-page stamp PDF, fitted and centred on every page, half transparent. byte[] paid = PdfStamper.Stamp(invoicePdf, paidStampPdf, new PdfStampOptions { Opacity = 0.5f }); // Letterhead under the content: the stamp's first page on page 1, its second page on all the others. byte[] letter = PdfStamper.Stamp(letterPdf, letterheadPdf, new PdfStampOptions { Underlay = true, MatchPages = true }); // Actual size in the top right corner, 20 pt in from each edge, on the first page only. byte[] copy = PdfStamper.Stamp(pdf, copyStampPdf, new PdfStampOptions { Position = PdfStampPosition.TopRight, Scale = 1, OffsetX = -20, OffsetY = 20, Pages = i => i == 0, }); // The stamp as HTML, rendered at each page's size with no margins. byte[] stamped = PdfStamper.StampHtml(pdf, "
PAID
"); PdfStamper.StampFile("in.pdf", "stamp.pdf", "out.pdf"); PdfStamper.Stamp(inputStream, stampStream, outputStream);

StampHtml renders the HTML with the options you pass but ignores their footer, header, watermark, attachments, bookmarks and tagging, so the main conversion's PdfOptions can be reused without drawing a second footer. StampPage picks the stamp PDF's page (0-based), Pages the pages to stamp (by 0-based index), Scale the size (0, the default, fits the stamp page on the page keeping its aspect ratio; 1 is its own size), and Position, OffsetX (right) and OffsetY (down) where it goes. The stamp is placed as the page is displayed, so it is upright on rotated pages and sits in the crop box. The stamp page is copied in once as a form XObject, so its text stays text and its graphics stay sharp, however many pages show it. The page's own content is wrapped so a graphics state it leaves behind cannot shift or recolour an overlay. Underlays are hidden by pages that paint an opaque background, and annotations (links, form fields) are always drawn above the page content, overlays included.

Everything else in the document is kept: annotations, form fields and their values, bookmarks, named destinations, attachments, metadata, page labels and the structure tree of a tagged PDF, in which the stamp is marked as an artifact (a PDF/UA-1 document stamped this way still passes veraPDF, as does a PDF/A-2b one when the stamp has embedded fonts). The stamp page's own annotations, form fields and tags are not copied. The result is written out in full, not as an incremental update. A signed PDF is refused with InvalidOperationException, since stamping would break the signatures; set InvalidateSignatures = true to stamp it anyway, or stamp before signing. Encrypted inputs open with Password (and StampPassword for the stamp); the result is not encrypted unless Security is set. Both inputs are handled as untrusted, like merge inputs: damaged files are repaired where possible, decoding is limited, and an unreadable file or one without pages throws InvalidDataException.

PdfCompactor makes an existing PDF smaller, any PDF, not only those PdfPecker made. By default nothing visible changes: the pages, bookmarks, links, forms, tags, attachments and PDF/A and PDF/UA conformance are kept, and every image keeps its exact pixels. // Lossless: the same pages, in fewer bytes. byte[] smaller = PdfCompactor.Compact(File.ReadAllBytes("merged.pdf")); // Smaller still: images above 150 dpi downsampled, and photos recompressed as JPEG at quality 75. byte[] smallest = PdfCompactor.Compact(pdf, new PdfCompactOptions { MaxImageDpi = 150, ImageQuality = 75 }); // Streams in and out; nothing is written when the input cannot be compacted. PdfCompactor.Compact(inputStream, outputStream);

The document is written out again with only the objects its pages and catalog still use, so earlier revisions kept by incremental updates and orphaned objects go. Identical objects are stored once, such as the same font or image embedded many times, which merging documents often leaves behind. Streams with lossless filters are recompressed at the strongest Flate level, with PNG predictors for images, whenever that is smaller; JPEG, JPEG 2000, JBIG2 and CCITT images keep their data. Objects are written in minimal syntax and packed into compressed object streams. The result depends only on the input and the options, so the same PDF always gives the same bytes. When rewriting does not make the file smaller, the input comes back unchanged.

Option Default What it does ImageQuality null Re-encodes 8-bit greyscale and RGB images as JPEG at this quality (1 to 100) where that makes them smaller. 75 to 85 suits most documents. This is lossy, also for images that were not JPEGs, such as screenshots and logos. MaxImageDpi null Downsamples 8-bit greyscale and RGB images drawn at a higher resolution than this, judged by the largest size each image is drawn at on any page. A downsampled JPEG is re-encoded as JPEG (at ImageQuality, or 85); other images stay lossless unless ImageQuality is set. 150 suits the screen, 300 print. RemoveMetadata false Removes the document information (title, author, dates) and XMP metadata. They are kept when the PDF claims PDF/A or PDF/UA, which require them. RemoveApplicationData true Removes page thumbnails, which viewers draw themselves, and the private data editing applications keep in the file (/PieceInfo, such as Illustrator's editable copy), which no viewer shows. UseObjectStreams true Packs objects into compressed object streams with a cross-reference stream (PDF 1.5, which every current reader supports). Turn it off for readers from before 2003. PDF/A-1 files never use them, as PDF/A-1 does not allow them. An overload takes a CancellationToken, which stops the work between objects.

Digitally signed PDFs are refused with ArgumentException, because rewriting them breaks the signatures. Compact before signing instead. Encrypted PDFs are refused too, since a rewrite would drop their protection: decrypt with PdfProtector.Decrypt, compact, and encrypt the result again with PdfProtector.Encrypt (see PDF/A, passwords and watermarks). A file that is not a readable PDF throws InvalidDataException.

PdfText extracts the text of any PDF, not only those PdfPecker made, in reading order: as one string, or page by page with every line and word and where it is on the page. It reads what the PDF draws, using PdfPecker's own PDF parser and font engines, so it needs no other package either. // All the text, pages separated by a form feed (\f) as pdftotext does. string text = PdfText.Extract(pdfBytes); string report = PdfText.ExtractFile("report.pdf"); // Some pages of an encrypted PDF. string summary = PdfText.Extract(pdfBytes, new PdfTextOptions { Password = "pw", Pages = PdfPageRange.Parse("1-3") }); // Lines and words with their positions, such as for finding a total on an invoice. foreach (PdfTextPage page in PdfText.ExtractPages(pdfBytes)) foreach (PdfTextLine line in page.Lines) if (line.Text.StartsWith("Total")) Console.WriteLine($"Page {page.PageNumber}, {line.Y:F0} pt from the top: {line.Words[^1].Text}"); PdfTextPage first = PdfText.ExtractPage(pdfBytes, 1); Extract, ExtractPages and ExtractPage also take a Stream, and ExtractPagesFromFile reads the pages of a file.

PdfTextPage.Text is the page's text, with lines separated by a line feed and paragraphs by an empty line. Its Lines go from top to bottom, and each PdfTextLine has its Text, its Words in reading order and a bounding box (X, Y, Width, Height). Each PdfTextWord has its Text, its box, its FontSize and its FontName (such as Helvetica-Bold). Positions are in points from the top-left corner of the page as it is displayed, after its rotation, with y growing downward, like the signature box and the stamp offsets. Boxes span the font's usual ascent and descent, so they are close to, not exactly, the inked area. Text that runs up or down the page gets its own lines, with their Angle.

The characters come from the fonts' ToUnicode maps, encodings and glyph names, for the standard fonts and for embedded TrueType, CFF, Type 1 and Type 3 fonts, and /ActualText in marked content stands for the glyphs it covers. Where a PDF draws no space between words but leaves a gap, the gap becomes a space; kerning and letter spacing do not. Ligatures such as ﬁ come out as their letters unless ExpandLigatures is false. Right-to-left text such as Arabic and Hebrew comes out in logical order, and PdfTextLine.RightToLeft says when most of a line is. Invisible text, such as the recognised text layer of a scanned page, is included, and text hidden by optional content (a layer that is off) is not. The values shown in form fields and the text of stamps are included unless IncludeAnnotations is false. Pages are read in parallel (MaxDegreeOfParallelism, default one per processor), MaxPages (default 100,000) limits the work, and inputs are handled as untrusted, as with merging. A damaged file or page throws InvalidDataException, a wrong password PdfPasswordException. Columns side by side are read across, line by line, not one column after the other, and table cells on one row make one line. Text drawn only as outlines or images has no characters to extract; a scanned page needs OCR first. See Limitations.

PdfToImage and PdfRenderer render PDF pages to PNG, JPEG, WebP or TIFF (or raw RGBA pixels). This works for any PDF, not only PdfPecker's own output, and also uses no third-party packages: the PDF parser, font engines, JPEG and fax decoders, rasterizer and the PNG, JPEG, WebP and TIFF encoders are all part of the library. // Every page as PNG bytes (rendered in parallel), or one page (0-based index) byte[][] pages = PdfToImage.Convert(pdfBytes, new ImageOptions { Dpi = 150 }); byte[] first = PdfToImage.ConvertPage(pdfBytes, 0); // report.pdf -> out/report-1.png, out/report-2.png, ... PdfToImage.ConvertFile("report.pdf", "out"); // JPEG or lossless WebP: report.pdf -> out/report-1.jpg, ... (or .webp) PdfToImage.ConvertFile("report.pdf", "out", new ImageOptions { Format = PdfImageFormat.Jpeg, Quality = 90 }); byte[][] webps = PdfToImage.Convert(pdfBytes, new ImageOptions { Format = PdfImageFormat.WebP }); // Open once, render many pages; RenderedImage also exposes the RGBA pixels var renderer = PdfRenderer.Open(pdfBytes, password: null); RenderedImage image = renderer.RenderPage(2, new ImageOptions { Width = 800 }); image.SavePng("page3.png"); File.WriteAllBytes("page3.jpg", image.ToJpeg(quality: 85)); File.WriteAllBytes("page3.webp", image.ToWebP()); // The whole PDF as one multi-page TIFF, here black and white for fax or archiving byte[] tiff = PdfToImage.ConvertToTiff(pdfBytes, new ImageOptions { Dpi = 200, TiffColorMode = TiffColorMode.BlackAndWhite }); PdfToImage.ConvertFileToTiff("report.pdf", "report.tif");

HtmlToImage converts HTML straight to one image per page, for previews, thumbnails and e-mails. It is the shortcut for HtmlToPdf.Convert followed by PdfToImage.Convert, takes the same PdfOptions and ImageOptions, and gives the same images. Security and Signature are ignored, since they change nothing on the page. byte[][] pages = HtmlToImage.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.A4 }, new ImageOptions { Dpi = 96 }); byte[][] jpegs = await HtmlToImage.ConvertAsync(html, imageOptions: new ImageOptions { Format = PdfImageFormat.Jpeg });

Output formats (ImageOptions.Format, default Png; RenderedImage.Encode()/Save() use it too): PNG: lossless, RGB for opaque pages and RGBA otherwise. JPEG: baseline JFIF with the standard (IJG) quantisation tables scaled by Quality (1 to 100, default 85) and Huffman tables optimised per image. Below quality 90 colour is subsampled 4:2:0; from 90 it keeps full resolution (4:4:4), which keeps coloured text sharp. JPEG has no transparency, so a Transparent render is flattened onto BackgroundColor (white by default). At quality 90 a 150 DPI text page decodes at about 45 dB PSNR. WebP: always lossless (VP8L), alpha included, decoding to exactly the PNG's pixels and usually 50% to 70% smaller. Pages with up to 256 colours use a palette (packed 2, 4 or 8 pixels per byte when small); others use subtract-green and per-tile prediction, then LZ77, a colour cache and canonical prefix codes. Here Quality is the compression effort (default 29): higher spends more time searching for a smaller file and never changes a pixel; 85, the default before 1.19.0, makes files about 1% smaller and takes nearly twice as long. Lossy WebP is not written. WebP is limited to 16,384 pixels per side (JPEG to 65,535); larger images throw NotSupportedException. TIFF: lossless, one page per file with Format = PdfImageFormat.Tiff (.tif from ConvertFile, or RenderedImage.ToTiff()), or every page in one multi-page file with ConvertToTiff, ConvertToTiffAsync, ConvertFileToTiff and PdfRenderer.RenderAllToTiff. See TIFF.

ImageOptions.TiffColorMode picks Color (the default: RGB, or RGBA when the render is transparent), Grayscale or BlackAndWhite. TiffCompression defaults to CCITT Group 4 for black and white and LZW otherwise; None, Lzw, Deflate, PackBits and CcittGroup4 (always black and white) can be set, and all of them are lossless. For black and white, TiffThreshold (1 to 255, default 128) is the brightness below which a pixel becomes black. Greyscale and black and white flatten transparency onto BackgroundColor, and Dpi is written into the file so it prints at the right size. Files are classic TIFF, so output over 4 GB throws NotSupportedException (BigTIFF is not written). // Greyscale archive copy with Deflate byte[] archive = PdfToImage.ConvertToTiff(pdfBytes, new ImageOptions { Dpi = 300, TiffColorMode = TiffColorMode.Grayscale, TiffCompression = TiffCompression.Deflate, });

ImageOptions sets Dpi (default 150) or a target Width/Height in pixels, BackgroundColor or Transparent, RenderAnnotations, Password, MaxDegreeOfParallelism, PngCompression, Format, Quality (85 for JPEG and 29 for WebP until it is set; an ArgumentOutOfRangeException outside 1 to 100) and the TIFF options. A PdfRenderer is thread-safe and shares decoded fonts and images between pages. Encrypted files open with the user or owner password (PdfPasswordException otherwise); unreadable files throw InvalidDataException, as does a page that needs more than 20 million drawing operations (nested forms can multiply a few bytes into billions). Pass a cancellation token to bound the time a page may take.

Files: cross-reference tables and streams, object streams, incremental updates, damaged files (rebuilt by scanning), RC4 and AES-128/256 encryption, all standard filters (Flate, LZW, ASCII85, ASCIIHex, RunLength, predictors). Graphics: paths, fills (non-zero and even-odd), strokes with joins, caps and dashes, clipping, anti-aliasing, all blend modes, constant alpha, soft masks, transparency groups, axial, radial, function and mesh shadings (types 1 to 7), tiling patterns, form XObjects, optional content (layers) and annotation appearances. Text: embedded TrueType, OpenType, CFF and Type 1 fonts, Type 3 fonts, CID fonts with CMaps, vertical text, all text rendering modes. The 14 standard fonts and non-embedded fonts are drawn with built-in Liberation and DejaVu-derived faces stretched to the document's widths. Images: every bit depth and colour space (Gray, RGB, CMYK, Lab, ICC-based, Indexed, Separation, DeviceN), baseline and progressive JPEG, JPEG 2000 (JPXDecode, including embedded alpha), JBIG2 (generic, text, symbol, refinement and halftone regions, with JBIG2Globals), CCITT fax, stencil masks, colour-key masks and soft masks. For what the renderer does not support yet, see Limitations.

PdfToHtml turns any PDF, not only those PdfPecker made, into one HTML file that looks like the PDF. Each page is an image of the page, and the page's text is laid invisibly over it word by word, so it can be selected, copied, found with the browser's search and read by screen readers. The PDF's web, mail and phone links and its links between pages keep working. Use it to show statements, invoices or reports in a web page or an e-mail portal without a PDF viewer. // Any PDF as one self-contained HTML page string html = PdfToHtml.Convert(File.ReadAllBytes("statement.pdf")); // File to file, or straight to a stream a few pages at a time, so a long PDF is never held in memory whole PdfToHtml.ConvertFile("report.pdf", "report.html"); using (var file = File.Create("report.html")) PdfToHtml.Convert(pdfBytes, file); // Some pages of an encrypted PDF, as sharper JPEG images string first = PdfToHtml.Convert(pdfBytes, new PdfHtmlOptions { Password = "pw", Pages = PdfPageRange.Parse("1-3"), Dpi = 200, ImageFormat = PdfImageFormat.Jpeg, Quality = 80, }); Convert also takes a Stream, and every method takes a CancellationToken.

The output is one self-contained HTML file with no scripts: the page images, the style sheet and the small web font of the text layer are all inside it, so it can be saved, mailed or served as it is. Pages scale to the width of the window, down to a phone screen, and print on paper of their own size. Every page is a div with the class pdf-page and the id page- followed by its page number, so report.html#page-3 opens the third page. The pages are drawn by PdfPecker's own PDF renderer and the text comes from text extraction, so everything those can read works here: any fonts, JPEG 2000, JBIG2 and CCITT images, encrypted PDFs, form fields and annotations. Pages are converted in parallel.

PdfHtmlOptions Default Password none The user or owner password of an encrypted PDF Pages every page The pages to convert, such as PdfPageRange.Parse("1-3") Dpi 150 The resolution of the page images; higher is sharper on high-density screens and makes larger files ImageFormat WebP WebP (lossless), Png, or Jpeg (smaller for photos and scans, but lossy) Quality 85 for JPEG, 29 for WebP The JPEG quality, or the WebP compression effort, from 1 to 100; WebP never loses a pixel, and 85 (the default before 1.19.0) makes it about 1% smaller and slower IncludeText true Lay the text invisibly over the images IncludeLinks true Turn web, mail, phone and page links into links; javascript: and file links are always left out RenderAnnotations true Draw form fields, stamps and comments, and include their text Title the PDF's title The HTML document's title MaxDimension 16,384 The most pixels on either side of a page image; larger pages get a lower resolution MaxPages 10,000 More pages throw PdfLimitException MaxDegreeOfParallelism processor count The most pages converted at the same time

The HTML keeps the PDF's layout rather than reflowing it into paragraphs and tables, and the text is shown in the image rather than in the PDF's fonts, so it zooms as an image does. Text that the PDF draws only as outlines or images, such as a scan, can be seen but not selected, since there is no OCR. See Limitations.

wkhtmltopdf was archived in January 2023 and gets no more fixes, security fixes included. It renders with a Qt WebKit engine from 2016, so flexbox, grid and most CSS written since then don't work, and it has to be deployed as a native binary of about 90 MB for each operating system. .NET wrappers such as DinkToPdf, Rotativa, NReco.PdfGenerator and WkHtmlToPdf-DotNet carry the same engine with them. PdfPecker is a replacement written in plain C#. It is one NuGet package with no native files, it supports modern CSS, and it converts in your own process instead of starting a program for every PDF. It is free under the MIT license. dotnet add package PdfPecker

From the command line or a Process // Before: one wkhtmltopdf process per document var process = Process.Start("wkhtmltopdf", "--page-size A4 -T 20mm -B 20mm invoice.html invoice.pdf"); process.WaitForExit(); // After using PdfPecker; HtmlToPdf.ConvertFile("invoice.html", "invoice.pdf", new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.A4, Margins = PageMargins.FromMillimeters(20, 10, 20, 10), }); From DinkToPdf or WkHtmlToPdf-DotNet // Before var converter = new SynchronizedConverter(new PdfTools()); var document = new HtmlToPdfDocument { GlobalSettings = { PaperSize = PaperKind.A4, Orientation = Orientation.Landscape }, Objects = { new ObjectSettings { HtmlContent = html } }, }; byte[] pdf = converter.Convert(document); // After byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.A4.Landscape }); There is no converter object to keep alive and no native library to load: HtmlToPdf is static and thread-safe, so many requests can convert at the same time without the SynchronizedConverter lock. From Rotativa in ASP.NET Core Rotativa renders a Razor view and passes the HTML to wkhtmltopdf. Render the view to a string the way you already do for emails, or build the HTML from a template, and return the PDF: app.MapGet("/invoice/{id}", (int id) => Results.File(HtmlToPdf.Convert(RenderInvoice(id)), "application/pdf", $"invoice-{id}.pdf"));

wkhtmltopdf PdfPecker --page-size A4, -O Landscape PageSize = PageSize.A4.Landscape, or CSS @page { size: A4 landscape } -T, -R, -B, -L Margins = PageMargins.FromMillimeters(top, right, bottom, left), or CSS @page { margin: ... } --footer-center "[page] of [topage]" FooterText = "{page} of {pages}", or an @page margin box with counter(page) and counter(pages) --header-html header.html An element with data-sticky-pdf-header in the page (see Paged media) --title Title, or the document's <title> --outline On by default: bookmarks come from h1 to h6 toc Write the table of contents in your HTML with target-counter() and leader() for page numbers --print-media-type Always on: @media print rules apply --enable-local-file-access Files under BaseDirectory are read; AllowFileAccess = true allows others --zoom, smart shrinking Scale. PdfPecker does not shrink content to fit, so check page breaks after switching --javascript-delay, --run-script Not supported: render the content into the HTML before converting --enable-forms On by default: inputs become fillable fields (FormFields = false turns it off)

Pages can count differently. wkhtmltopdf shrinks content to fit the page by default, so a report that was 24 pages can become 29 at its real size. Set Scale if you need the old size back, but the real size is usually what the CSS meant. Flexbox, grid, calc(), CSS variables and other modern CSS now work, so workarounds written for the old WebKit, such as tables used for layout or -webkit-box, can be removed or left as they are. JavaScript is not run. Charts or text that scripts add to the page have to be in the HTML already, for example as SVG made on the server. Fonts come from files you register, not from the server's installed fonts, so the output is the same on every machine. See Fonts.

On the same 4-core Linux VM, a one-page invoice took 282 ms with wkhtmltopdf and 0.92 ms with PdfPecker, and a 30-page report 600 ms and 33 ms. Deployment drops from about 90 MB of native files to one 5 MB DLL. The full comparison is on the Performance page.

HTML to PDF in C#: a walk-through with templates, ASP.NET Core and fonts. HTML and CSS and Limitations: what your templates can use. Compare: PdfPecker next to wkhtmltopdf and the other .NET converters, feature by feature.

HtmlRenderer.PdfSharp is a free, managed HTML to PDF converter that runs on top of PDFsharp. Two things make people look for a replacement: The licence of the engine underneath. HtmlRenderer.PdfSharp 1.6.1 itself is BSD-licensed and still installs PDFsharp 6.2.4, the last MIT version. PDFsharp 6.5.0 (October 2026) and the 7.0 previews are AGPL-3.0 or a paid commercial licence. Updating PDFsharp, by hand or with a tool such as Dependabot, adding another package that needs a newer PDFsharp, or a future HtmlRenderer release built on it, brings in the AGPL, which requires you to publish your own application's source code unless you buy a licence. Staying on MIT means pinning PDFsharp at 6.2.4 and doing without its future fixes. The CSS. HtmlRenderer supports HTML 4 and CSS 2, so flexbox, grid, CSS variables, calc() and @page rules are ignored. PdfPecker is also fully managed and runs in your own process, with no dependencies at all, under the MIT licence. It supports modern CSS and has PDF/A, PDF/UA, signatures, forms and merging built in. dotnet add package PdfPecker Then remove the HtmlRenderer.PdfSharp package, and PDFsharp too if nothing else in your project uses it.

// Before using PdfSharp; using TheArtOfDev.HtmlRenderer.PdfSharp; var document = PdfGenerator.GeneratePdf(html, PageSize.A4); document.Save("invoice.pdf"); // After using PdfPecker; File.WriteAllBytes("invoice.pdf", HtmlToPdf.Convert(html)); A4 is the default. With margins and a page footer: // Before var config = new PdfGenerateConfig { PageSize = PageSize.A4, MarginTop = 40, MarginBottom = 40 }; var document = PdfGenerator.GeneratePdf(html, config); // After byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { Margins = PageMargins.FromMillimeters(14, 15, 14, 15), FooterText = "Page {page} of {pages}", }); HtmlRenderer has no page numbers of its own; PdfPecker has FooterText, @page margin boxes and running headers and footers written in HTML (see Paged media).

HtmlRenderer.PdfSharp PdfPecker PageSize, PageOrientation in PdfGenerateConfig PageSize = PageSize.A4.Landscape, or CSS @page { size: A4 landscape } MarginTop, MarginBottom, MarginLeft, MarginRight (points) Margins = new PageMargins(top, right, bottom, left) in points, or PageMargins.FromMillimeters cssData argument UserStyleSheet, or <style> and <link> in the HTML imageLoad and stylesheetLoad events ResourceResolver, or files under BaseDirectory PdfDocument for further editing PDF bytes; merge, stamp, sign and protect them with PdfPecker's own APIs Fonts from PDFsharp's GlobalFontSettings.FontResolver options.Fonts.AddFile(...) or @font-face (see Fonts)

Modern CSS now works. Layouts built with tables and floats to suit CSS 2 keep working, and you can move to flexbox and grid when you want. Backgrounds and colours that HtmlRenderer dropped, such as coloured table headers, are drawn. Long tables break across pages with their header row repeated, and rows are never cut in half. Text is laid out by PdfPecker's own engine, so line breaks and page breaks can fall in slightly different places. Check your longest templates after switching.

On the same 4-core Linux VM, a one-page invoice took 4.9 ms with HtmlRenderer.PdfSharp and 0.92 ms with PdfPecker, a 30-page report 360 ms and 33 ms, and peak memory was 255 MB and 92 MB. See Performance.

h: When HtmlRenderer is still a fine choice
x: For simple HTML that already looks right, there is no urgent reason to move today: version 1.6.1 runs on the MIT PDFsharp 6.2.4. Pin that version so an update can't change the licence. PDFsharp itself remains a solid API for drawing PDFs from code. Compare shows the two side by side with the other .NET converters.

IronPDF converts HTML with an embedded Chrome engine and is sold per developer. PdfPecker converts the same kind of templates with its own engine written in C#: no Chrome binaries to deploy, no licence key, and an MIT licence that is free for commercial use. For invoices, payslips, reports and other HTML you control, the output can match IronPDF's to a fraction of a millimetre. dotnet add package PdfPecker

// Before var renderer = new ChromePdfRenderer(); renderer.RenderingOptions.PaperSize = PdfPaperSize.A4; renderer.RenderingOptions.MarginTop = 20; renderer.RenderingOptions.MarginBottom = 20; renderer.RenderingOptions.TextFooter = new TextHeaderFooter { CenterText = "{page} of {total-pages}" }; using var document = renderer.RenderHtmlAsPdf(html); byte[] pdf = document.BinaryData; // After using PdfPecker; byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.A4, Margins = PageMargins.FromMillimeters(20, 15, 20, 15), FooterText = "{page} of {pages}", }); HtmlToPdf is static and thread-safe, so there is no renderer to create or dispose, and conversions can run in parallel. To write the PDF to a file or a response stream, pass the stream: HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, stream).

IronPDF's HtmlHeaderFooter takes a piece of HTML with {page} and {total-pages}. In PdfPecker the header or footer is an element of the page itself, marked with data-sticky-pdf-header or data-sticky-pdf-footer, and the same placeholders work:
ACME Ltd
...
Page {page} of {total-pages}
The element is drawn on every page and the content flows between them. See Paged media for @page margin boxes and running headers.

Chrome lays a page out at a whole number of CSS pixels and stretches it to the paper, so IronPDF's PDFs are a little larger than the CSS says. If you are switching an existing system and want every box and glyph where IronPDF put it, for example to compare old and new PDFs, use the same page geometry: var options = new PdfOptions { PageSize = new PageSize(594.96f, 841.92f), // A4 as Chrome writes it Scale = 793.28f / 793f, TruncateBandsToWholePoints = true, // header and footer heights rounded as Chrome does }; One user ran this on the 26 templates of their production app: 24 came out identical to IronPDF's output and the other two differed by less than 0.25 mm. For a new system, the defaults are fine.

On the same 26 production templates, IronPDF 2026.7.2 took 13.6 s for all of them one at a time and PdfPecker 17 ms. With 22 in parallel, IronPDF made 9.2 documents per second and PdfPecker 1,143. Details are on the Performance page.

h: When IronPDF is the better choice
x: IronPDF prints exactly what Chrome prints, runs JavaScript, converts live websites and comes with paid support and a large PDF editing API. If your pages build themselves with scripts, or you need output identical to a browser for arbitrary HTML, keep a Chrome-based converter. Compare lists what each converter can do.

PuppeteerSharp and Playwright make PDFs by driving a real Chromium browser. That gives exactly what Chrome prints, but it means downloading and patching a browser of about 600 MB, keeping it running, and paying for a browser tab for every document. PdfPecker converts HTML to PDF in your own process with its own engine written in C#, so there is no browser to install and a one-page document takes about a millisecond. It is free under the MIT license. dotnet add package PdfPecker

From PuppeteerSharp // Before await new BrowserFetcher().DownloadAsync(); await using var browser = await Puppeteer.LaunchAsync(new LaunchOptions { Headless = true }); await using var page = await browser.NewPageAsync(); await page.SetContentAsync(html); byte[] pdf = await page.PdfDataAsync(new PdfOptions { Format = PaperFormat.A4, PrintBackground = true, MarginOptions = new MarginOptions { Top = "20mm", Bottom = "20mm" }, }); // After using PdfPecker; byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.A4, Margins = PageMargins.FromMillimeters(20, 15, 20, 15), }); Both libraries have a class called PdfOptions, so in a project that still uses PuppeteerSharp elsewhere, write PdfPecker.PdfOptions. From Playwright // Before using var playwright = await Playwright.CreateAsync(); await using var browser = await playwright.Chromium.LaunchAsync(); var page = await browser.NewPageAsync(); await page.SetContentAsync(html); byte[] pdf = await page.PdfAsync(new PagePdfOptions { Format = "A4", PrintBackground = true }); // After byte[] pdf = await HtmlToPdf.ConvertAsync(html); A4 is the default page size. HtmlToPdf is static and thread-safe, so there is no browser to share between requests and nothing to dispose or restart.

Chrome's headerTemplate and footerTemplate use <span class="pageNumber"> and <span class="totalPages">, and need displayHeaderFooter. In PdfPecker, use FooterText = "{page} of {pages}" for a simple line, or put the header or footer in the page itself: <footer data-sticky-pdf-footer height="12mm">Page {page} of {total-pages}</footer> Unlike Chrome's templates, these elements use the page's own stylesheets, fonts and images. @page margin boxes with counter(page) work too. See Paged media.

JavaScript is not run, so content that scripts build in the browser has to be in the HTML before conversion. Templates rendered on the server (Razor, Scriban, string building) work as they are.
