On the same 4-core Linux VM, a one-page invoice took 106 ms with PuppeteerSharp, 131 ms with Playwright and 0.92 ms with PdfPecker. Peak memory was 813 MB and 1,027 MB for the browser-based converters and 92 MB for PdfPecker, and in parallel PdfPecker made 1,132 documents per second against 12 to 15. The full table is on the Performance page.

PuppeteerSharp and Playwright are free and print exactly what Chrome shows, so they remain the right tool for pages that build themselves with JavaScript, for live websites and for screenshots. Compare shows what each converter can do.

PdfPecker is built for fast conversion of HTML templates you control, not for rendering arbitrary web pages. These are the known gaps; most are scope choices for speed and size, and they are the first candidates for future work. Anything not listed in What is supported should be assumed missing. The PDF feature checklist marks every PDF feature as supported, partly supported or missing.

No JavaScript. Scripts are never run, so content must be in the HTML before conversion (render it server-side first). No network access: http:/https: stylesheets and images are not downloaded. Supply them through your ResourceResolver, as files under BaseDirectory, or as data: URIs. <canvas>, <iframe>, <video>, <audio>, <object> and <embed> are not drawn, nor are file, range, colour and image inputs. Form fields have no JavaScript (no calculations, formats or submit actions), and a field inside a transformed box, a running header or footer, or a position: fixed box is drawn but not fillable.

Without registered fonts or EmbedStandardFonts, text uses the standard PDF fonts, so characters are limited to the Windows-1252 set (Western European languages) plus what the built-in fallback fonts add: Central European, Greek and Cyrillic letters and common symbols. They have no CJK or other scripts, and no emoji: register fonts for those. Complex-script shaping covers Arabic and Hebrew (and other scripts written with Arabic letters, such as Persian and Urdu), nine Indic scripts, Thai and Lao. Khmer, Myanmar, Sinhala, Tibetan, Mongolian, Javanese, Adlam and Syriac are not shaped, so their vowel signs and conjuncts come out wrong. Thai and Lao text breaks only at spaces, since there is no dictionary for word breaks. Vertical text is drawn as turned horizontal text: Chinese and Japanese characters are turned rather than upright (text-orientation and text-combine-upright are not supported), vertical-lr stacks several lines right to left, a box nested inside a vertical box takes its width as its height, and a vertical html or body is laid out horizontally. vi and vb stay the page width and height in vertical boxes (Chrome swaps them), and initial-letter makes no drop cap in a vertical box. CJK punctuation trimming does not use the vertical vhal feature, and the text-spacing shorthand is not read. text-emphasis marks and hanging-punctuation are not supported. In Latin and other simple scripts, shaping is limited to kerning, standard ligatures and features that swap one glyph for another (see OpenType features) and fractions; contextual alternates (calt) and ordinals are not applied, and small-caps is synthesized from scaled capitals when the font has no small capitals of its own. font-variant-alternates and font-palette (colour font palettes) are not supported. Solid underlines, overlines and line-throughs are a little thinner than Chrome's (about 1.5 px for 20 px text where Chrome draws 2 px), and a solid overline sits about a pixel lower; dashed, dotted, double and wavy lines match Chrome. text-decoration on SVG text is always a solid line in the text's fill, and is not drawn on textPath text. Automatic hyphenation (hyphens: auto) has built-in patterns for English, Danish, German, Dutch, Norwegian, Swedish, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese and Polish; other languages need their patterns in PdfOptions.Hyphenation. SVG <text> uses only the first value of position lists; in a text chunk with right-to-left text, dx on its tspans is ignored.

Container queries: no scroll-state() queries, style() works only on custom properties, and style containment (counter scoping) and the contain property are not implemented. A document with container queries takes about two to four times as long to lay out, and queries that keep changing the layout stop after six passes. In running headers and footers, @page margin boxes and SVG images, the cq units fall back to viewport units. Footnotes: @footnote inside @page :first, :left or :right is ignored, footnote-policy: block acts like line, and footnote-display: compact is always inline. A note split across pages does not carry its background or border onto the next page, and margins between block notes do not collapse. When @page :first, :left or :right give pages different widths, floats, inline-blocks, flex, grid and multi-column containers, and boxes with transforms or filters keep the width of the page they start on (Chrome re-sizes floats, inline-blocks and multi-column per page). A named page's :first is the document's first page, as in Chrome, not the first page of the named run. Selectors: a rule with an unsupported selector is skipped. A complex selector may have at most 64 compound parts and 16 levels of nesting, and :has() cannot contain :has(). Blurred text shadows are drawn as images at 144 dpi (down to 72 dpi for wide blurs, with the blur capped at about 200px), so shadowing long body text adds to the file size; the shadow of an underline is painted under the glyphs rather than between them and their own underline. filter: blur() and drop-shadow() draw the box as an image; its text stays selectable, and the colour filters keep everything as vectors. text-overflow applies only at the end of the line, as in the spec and Chrome. inline-size, block-size and their min- and max- forms always mean width and height, also in vertical writing modes; the logical margins, paddings, insets and borders do follow writing-mode. Percentage heights still count as auto in a flexed item of a container that has only a min-height, against a table row's height on its own or a rowspanning cell, and in footnotes and running headers and footers. When pages differ in size, a box resolves its percentage height against the page it starts on and keeps that height if it breaks onto a page of another height (Chrome recomputes it there). background-attachment: fixed scrolls with the box, since paper has no scrolling viewport. Not supported: contain, content-visibility, cross-fade(), element(), paint(), env(), anchor(), attr() outside content, ::selection and :nth-col(). In @page margins and media queries, ex, ch and the other font units use the initial 16 px font. 3D transforms are drawn flat, since a PDF page has only flat transforms: a box with a perspective stays a rectangle or parallelogram where Chrome draws a trapezoid, only the parent's perspective counts, and nested preserve-3d scenes, such as a cube, do not come out the way a screen shows them. backdrop-filter draws what is behind the box as a 144 dpi image, up to 64 per document. A mask with more than 16 layers is ignored, and mask-clip: no-clip, stroke-box and view-box act as border-box. Float shapes: an SVG image in shape-outside falls back to the margin box, and image and path shapes are measured at 1 px per CSS pixel, up to 4 million pixels and a shape-margin of 1,024 px (beyond that the float keeps its rectangle). text-wrap: balance and pretty do not apply beside floats, with ::first-line, or on pages of different widths. display: contents: a link to the id of such an element finds no place on the page when its children are blocks, and in a tagged PDF the wrapper's own tag (a list or link around blocks) is left out; its children are tagged. Gradient stops that fade to transparent are mixed in unpremultiplied colours, so the middle of such a gradient is a little greyer than in Chrome. A document without a doctype is laid out in standards mode; Chrome uses quirks mode for it, which, among other things, ignores the first paragraph's top margin in the body.

Inset box shadows of inline elements (<span>) are not drawn. box-decoration-break applies to inline elements, not to blocks split across pages or columns. Inline boxes nested more than 16 deep are not decorated, and one layout paints at most 50,000 inline box fragments with a shared budget for their layers, shadows and outlines; past it, fragments show only their background colour. A translucent box shadow without blur is blended onto white rather than truly see-through. Blurs are drawn as bands, so very wide blurs may show faint steps when zoomed in.

Subgrid: percentage gaps, margins and padding on a subgrid resolve against the parent grid's width rather than the subgrid's area; subgrid items are not baseline-aligned with the parent's items; and only the horizontal writing-mode is supported. Multi-column: column-span: all works only on direct children of the multi-column box, and multi-column boxes nested more than two levels deep keep their children whole instead of splitting them. Footnotes inside columns are placed at their call and do not reserve space at the bottom of the column, orphans and widows are not applied to lines beside floats, and content that overflows a fixed-height multi-column box with overflow: hidden is clipped from view but stays in the PDF's text. Overflow: a positioned child with a z-index inside a clipping box stays stacked within that box. Collapsed table borders on col and colgroup are not drawn; borders on cells, rows, row groups and the table are.

No AVIF images: decoding them needs an AV1 video decoder, which is not planned. Convert them to WebP, PNG or JPEG. SVG filters are applied in pixels at 144 dpi, so filtered shapes become an image (text keeps an invisible, selectable copy). A missing image with alt text shows the text without Chrome's small broken-image icon, and a missing image without alt text or a size has no box rather than Chrome's 16 px icon box. An SVG symbol is not clipped to its viewport, and its preserveAspectRatio is always the default (xMidYMid meet).

Text extraction reads columns that sit side by side across, line by line, rather than one column after the other, and it does not use the structure tree of a tagged PDF to find the reading order. Text drawn only as outlines or images is not extracted; there is no OCR. Indic vowel signs drawn before their consonant come out in that visual order unless the PDF carries /ActualText. PDF to HTML keeps the PDF's layout: the page is an image and the text an invisible layer over it, so the HTML does not reflow into paragraphs and tables, text zooms as an image does, and what text extraction cannot read (outlines, scans) cannot be selected either. Form filling does not shape text, so values in Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari and other scripts that need shaping are stored but not drawn correctly. XFA forms are not filled: their XFA data is removed and the AcroForm fields are filled instead. Field JavaScript (calculations, formats) is not run. Signature verification counts the updates made after a signature but does not analyse them against its permissions (no DocMDP or FieldMDP change analysis), so it cannot tell an allowed form fill from a changed page. Revocation is checked only when RevocationMode asks the platform to, not from the OCSP responses and CRLs stored in the PDF.

Markdown: no math. Definition list terms are one line each (no several terms for one definition), and ~ does not start a definition. A footnote's text cannot hold another page-bottom footnote: a reference inside a footnote links to its note, and a note that only other notes reference is listed after the text. PdfRenderer (PDF to image): no predefined CJK CMaps or non-embedded CJK fonts, and ICC profiles are not applied (ICC-based colours use their device equivalents). WebP output is lossless only (no lossy VP8), and JPEG output is baseline only (no progressive or arithmetic coding).

What the PDF format and other PDF libraries offer, and whether PdfPecker does it. Of the 133 features below, PdfPecker supports 82, supports 17 in part and leaves out 34. Some of those are left out on purpose, such as JavaScript in PDFs and the old RC4 encryption. The limitations page has the details of what is missing in HTML and CSS.

The PDF file itself: versions, cross-reference tables, pages and their boxes. Feature PdfPecker Notes Write PDF 1.4 and 1.7 ✓ Yes 1.4 for plain output, 1.7 when tagged, encrypted or PDF/A. Write PDF 2.0 ✓ Yes Used for PDF/A-4 and PDF/UA-2 output. Compressed object streams and xref streams ✓ Yes PdfCompactor packs objects into them; HtmlToPdf writes a classic xref table. Incremental updates ✓ Yes Signing and long-term validation append to the file, so earlier signatures stay valid. Linearization (Fast Web View) ✕ No Not written; a viewer must load the whole file before showing page 1. Open damaged files ✓ Yes Rebuilds a broken cross-reference table from the object headers. Page sizes, orientation and @page ✓ Yes A4, Letter, Legal, A3, A5, any custom size, landscape, and per-page sizes from CSS @page. Page rotation ✓ Yes PdfPages.Rotate on existing files; /Rotate is honoured when rendering. Page boxes (Crop, Bleed, Trim, Art) ½ Partly CropBox is read and kept. Bleed, trim and art boxes are not written, and CSS bleed and marks (crop marks) are ignored. Very large documents ✓ Yes Streaming merge and MaxPages limits; the readers have resource limits for hostile input.

Ways to produce a new PDF. Feature PdfPecker Notes HTML and CSS to PDF ✓ Yes Own parser, CSS engine and layout: flexbox, grid, tables, floats, multi-column, SVG and more. Markdown to PDF ✓ Yes CommonMark 0.31 and GitHub Flavored Markdown, with footnotes. Images to PDF ✓ Yes PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP and TIFF, one per page. Fluent C# API ✓ Yes PdfPecker.Fluent, in the style of QuestPDF. Headers, footers and page numbers ✓ Yes Running bands, @page margin boxes, {page} and {pages} tokens, and a different or no header and footer on the first page. Table of contents with page numbers ✓ Yes target-counter() and leader() from CSS Paged Media. Footnotes ✓ Yes CSS float: footnote, and Markdown footnotes at the page bottom. Scale content to fit a box ✓ Yes -pdfpecker-scale-to-fit: shrink for labels, badges and certificates. Barcodes and QR codes ✓ Yes QR, EPC payment QR, Code 128 and EAN-13, drawn as vectors. Content rendered by JavaScript ✕ No By design: no scripts run. Render the HTML on the server first. Low-level drawing API ✕ No There is no canvas-style API to draw paths and text at coordinates; content comes from HTML, Markdown, images or the fluent API.

How text is stored, so it looks right and stays searchable. Feature PdfPecker Notes Standard 14 fonts ✓ Yes Used by default; EmbedStandardFonts embeds metric-compatible fonts instead. TrueType and OpenType (CFF) embedding ✓ Yes Subset to the glyphs used. WOFF and WOFF2 web fonts ✓ Yes Decoded by the library's own WOFF2 decoder. Variable fonts ✓ Yes Instanced at the weight and width the CSS asks for. Copyable, searchable Unicode text ✓ Yes ToUnicode maps on every embedded font. Kerning, ligatures and OpenType features ✓ Yes Numerals, fractions, small capitals, super and subscripts. Complex scripts ½ Partly Arabic, Hebrew, nine Indic scripts, Thai and Lao are shaped. Khmer, Myanmar, Sinhala, Tibetan and others are not. Vertical text ½ Partly Drawn as turned horizontal text; CJK characters are not set upright. Fallback fonts ✓ Yes Bundled fonts for Central European, Greek, Cyrillic and symbols when your fonts lack a character. Colour fonts and emoji ✕ No COLR/CPAL, SVG and bitmap colour glyphs are not drawn. Outlined and stroked text ✓ Yes -webkit-text-stroke and paint-order, written as PDF text render modes.

What can be drawn on a page. Feature PdfPecker Notes Vector paths and inline SVG ✓ Yes SVG becomes PDF vector paths, not pictures. Gradients ✓ Yes Linear, radial and conic gradients as PDF shadings. Transparency, soft masks and blend modes ✓ Yes Opacity, mask-image, mix-blend-mode, isolation. Clipping ✓ Yes overflow, border-radius, clip-path. Tiling patterns ✓ Yes Repeated backgrounds and SVG patterns. Images: JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TIFF ✓ Yes JPEG is passed through unchanged; PNG alpha becomes a soft mask. AVIF images ✕ No Needs an AV1 decoder, which is not planned. sRGB output intent ✓ Yes Written for PDF/A. CMYK ½ Partly CMYK JPEGs are embedded (converted to RGB for PDF/A). There is no CSS device-cmyk() colour, so text and shapes are always RGB. Spot colours (Separation, DeviceN) ✕ No Not written. Read and rendered in existing PDFs. Overprint control ✕ No Not written, and not simulated when rendering. Filters and blur ½ Partly CSS filter, backdrop-filter and blurred shadows; blurs are drawn as 144 dpi images, colour filters stay vectors.

What a reader can click or open in a viewer. Feature PdfPecker Notes Bookmarks (outlines) ✓ Yes Built from h1 to h6; kept and nested when merging. Internal links ✓ Yes Links to #ids jump to the right page and position. External web links ✓ Yes URI link annotations. Named destinations ½ Partly Read when rendering and converting to HTML. New files use direct page destinations instead of a /Dests name tree. Page labels (i, ii, iii, A-1) ½ Partly Kept when merging; not written for new documents. Viewer preferences ½ Partly Display title and right-to-left direction are set. Page mode, page layout and an open action (start page or zoom) are not. Annotations ½ Partly Links and form widgets are written. Notes, highlights, stamps, free text, ink and shapes cannot be created. Existing ones are rendered and their text extracted. Layers (optional content) ½ Partly Not created. Existing layers are kept on merge and their visibility is honoured when rendering. JavaScript in the PDF ✕ No By design: no document or field scripts. Page transitions and presentation mode ✕ No Multimedia, 3D and rich media ✕ No Sound, video, 3D models and RichMedia annotations. PDF portfolios (collections) ✕ No Article threads ✕ No

Fillable fields. Feature PdfPecker Notes Create fields from HTML ✓ Yes Text, multi-line, password, checkbox, radio group, drop-down, list box and button. Read fields of any PDF ✓ Yes Name, type, value, options, flags and page. Fill fields ✓ Yes With new appearance streams, optionally with your own font. Flatten fields ✓ Yes Turn the fields into ordinary page content. Field calculations, formats and validation ✕ No These need JavaScript. Submit and reset actions ✕ No XFA forms ✕ No XFA data is removed when filling; the AcroForm fields are filled instead. Fill in complex scripts ½ Partly Arabic, Hebrew and Indic values are stored but not shaped in the appearance.

Passwords, permissions and protection. Feature PdfPecker Notes AES-256 encryption ✓ Yes Standard security handler revision 6, on new or existing PDFs. User and owner passwords ✓ Yes Permissions ✓ Yes Print, high-quality print, copy, modify, annotate, fill forms, assemble, accessibility. Open encrypted PDFs ✓ Yes RC4 40 to 128 bit, AES-128 and AES-256 (revisions 2 to 6). Remove a password ✓ Yes PdfProtector.Decrypt. Write RC4 or AES-128 ✕ No Only the current AES-256 is written, on purpose. Certificate (public-key) encryption ✕ No The Adobe.PubSec handler is not supported. Redaction ✕ No No way to remove content under a region. Sanitising ½ Partly PdfCompactor can drop metadata and application data; there is no full sanitise (scripts, hidden layers).

Signing and checking signatures. Feature PdfPecker Notes PAdES and PKCS#7 detached signatures ✓ Yes ETSI.CAdES.detached and adbe.pkcs7.detached. RSA, RSA-PSS and ECDSA keys ✓ Yes SHA-256 and other hash algorithms. Visible signature box ✓ Yes Page, position, size, text and border. External signers ✓ Yes HSMs, smart cards, PKCS#11 tokens and cloud signing services, also async. RFC 3161 timestamps ✓ Yes From the timestamp server you name. Document timestamps ✓ Yes Long-term validation ✓ Yes DSS and VRI with OCSP and CRL data, PAdES B-LT and B-LTA. Several signatures ✓ Yes Each signature is an incremental update, so earlier ones stay valid. Verify signatures ✓ Yes Byte range, digest, signature, timestamp and certificate chain. Certification signatures (DocMDP) ✕ No Cannot sign as the certifying author with change permissions. Change analysis ✕ No Verification counts updates after a signature but does not judge whether they were allowed. Revocation checks during verification ½ Partly Uses the platform's online check; the OCSP and CRL data stored in the PDF is not used.

ISO and industry profiles. Feature PdfPecker Notes PDF/A-1 ✕ No Only PDF/A-2 and later. PDF/A-2b, 2u, 3b, 3u ✓ Yes Checked with veraPDF in CI. PDF/A-4 and PDF/A-4f ✓ Yes PDF/A level a (2a, 3a) ½ Partly Tagging is there (PDF/UA), but the level a conformance itself is not declared. PDF/A-4e (engineering) ✕ No Tagged PDF ✓ Yes Structure tree built from the HTML. PDF/UA-1 and PDF/UA-2 ✓ Yes Accessible PDFs, also combined with PDF/A. Factur-X and ZUGFeRD ✓ Yes All profiles from Minimum to Extended and XRechnung; embedded and read back. XRechnung, Peppol BIS 3.0 and OIOUBL XML ✓ Yes Built from invoice data, totals checked against EN 16931. PDF/X (print production) ✕ No No PDF/X-1a, X-3 or X-4. PDF/E and PDF/VT ✕ No

Information about the document and files inside it. Feature PdfPecker Notes Document properties ✓ Yes Title, author, subject, keywords, creator, producer, dates. Custom properties ✓ Yes XMP metadata ✓ Yes Document language ✓ Yes Reproducible output ✓ Yes A fixed CreationDate or SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH gives byte-identical files. Embedded files ✓ Yes Add, list and extract, with MIME type, description and PDF/A-3 relationship. File attachment annotations ✕ No Files can be attached to the document, not pinned to a spot on a page. Read document properties ✕ No No public API returns the title, author or XMP of an existing PDF.

Changing files you already have. Feature PdfPecker Notes Merge ✓ Yes Also streamed, with bookmarks, page labels and forms kept. Split ✓ Yes Extract, remove and reorder pages ✓ Yes Rotate pages ✓ Yes Stamp, overlay and underlay ✓ Yes Another PDF or HTML on every page, or selected pages. Watermarks ✓ Yes Text, image and SVG. Compress and optimise ✓ Yes Lossless recompression, duplicate fonts and images stored once, optional image downsampling. Add or remove a password ✓ Yes Edit existing text and content ✕ No No find-and-replace or content editing. Insert blank pages, crop or resize pages ✕ No N-up and imposition ✕ No Convert an existing PDF to PDF/A ✕ No Only new documents are made as PDF/A.

Getting things out of existing PDFs. Feature PdfPecker Notes Render pages to PNG, JPEG, WebP and TIFF ✓ Yes Multi-page TIFF in colour, greyscale or CCITT Group 4. All PDF image filters ✓ Yes Flate, LZW, RunLength, ASCII85, ASCIIHex, DCT, JPEG 2000, JBIG2 and CCITT. All font types ✓ Yes Type 1, CFF, TrueType, Type 3 and CID fonts. Fonts that are not embedded ½ Partly Standard fonts are substituted; CJK fonts and predefined CJK CMaps are not. All seven shading types ✓ Yes Function, axial, radial and the four mesh types. Colour spaces ✓ Yes Device, Cal, Lab, ICC-based, Indexed, Separation, DeviceN and Pattern. ICC colour management ½ Partly ICC-based colours use their device equivalents; profiles are not applied. Transparency groups, blend modes, soft masks ✓ Yes Annotation appearances ✓ Yes Can be switched off. Text extraction with positions ✓ Yes Pages, lines and words with coordinates, font and size. Reading order ½ Partly Columns side by side are read across; the structure tree is not used. OCR ✕ No Text in scans and outlines cannot be extracted. PDF to HTML ✓ Yes Page images with a selectable, searchable text layer and working links. Reflowing PDF to HTML ✕ No The HTML keeps the PDF's fixed layout. Extract images ✕ No PDF to Word, Excel or PowerPoint ✕ No
PdfPecker lays out documents in your own process, without a browser, so a typical one-page document takes about a millisecond. For memory and CPU per document, see System requirements.

The same three documents converted to A4 PDF by PdfPecker and six .NET alternatives, on one 4-core cloud VM (Intel Xeon @ 2.1 GHz, 260 MB L3, 16 GB, Linux, .NET 10.0.13). Times are medians after a 3-second warm-up, averaged over two runs; "first PDF" includes starting the browser where there is one. Parallel runs one conversion per core at once on the 5-page document. Peak memory is the proportional set size (PSS) of the whole process tree, so a browser's helper processes are included once and shared pages are not double-counted; .NET processes run with a 16 MB GC gen0 budget, as .NET would otherwise size it from the CPU cache. Converter Engine To deploy First PDF Invoice, 1 page Feature tour, 5 pages Report, 30 pages Parallel Peak memory PdfPecker own, managed 5.1 MB DLL 0.40 s 0.92 ms 2.9 ms 33 ms 1,132 docs/s 92 MB HtmlRenderer.PdfSharp 1.6.1 own, managed (CSS 2) 5.0 MB of DLLs 0.54 s 4.9 ms 16 ms 360 ms 114 docs/s 255 MB iText pdfHTML 6.3.4 own, managed 11 MB of DLLs 1.18 s 24 ms 132 ms 2.2 s 15 docs/s 707 MB wkhtmltopdf 0.12.6 Qt WebKit, native about 90 MB with Qt 0.33 s 282 ms 309 ms 600 ms 12 docs/s 165 MB PuppeteerSharp 25.13 Chromium 141 about 600 MB browser 1.15 s 106 ms 142 ms 496 ms 15 docs/s 813 MB Microsoft.Playwright 1.63 Chromium 141 browser + 135 MB driver 0.98 s 131 ms 167 ms 517 ms 12 docs/s 1,027 MB Syncfusion HTML to PDF 35.1.40 Chrome (Blink), bundled about 545 MB with Chrome 2.46 s 183 ms 236 ms 968 ms 3 docs/s 2,239 MB How to read it: PdfPecker is 50 to 200 times faster than the Chromium-based converters on the 1 and 5-page documents and 15 to 30 times faster on the 30-page report, and uses an eighth or less of their memory. Per-document overhead (a browser tab, a process start) dominates for the others on small documents. Output is not identical. Chromium is the reference for modern CSS and runs JavaScript, which PdfPecker does not. HtmlRenderer supports only HTML 4 and CSS 2 (it drops the invoice's table header colours), and wkhtmltopdf uses a 2016 WebKit, shrinks content to fit by default (24 pages for the report instead of 29) and was archived in 2023. iText pdfHTML lays out the documents itself, like PdfPecker, but its time grows faster than the page count: 132 ms for 5 pages and 2.2 s for the 30-page report, which is one long table. Syncfusion ran as a trial without a licence key, which adds a line of text to each page. Its AdditionalDelay (2 seconds of waiting for scripts by default) was set to 0, as the other Chromium converters don't wait either. With its default settings it scales content down, so the report took 13 pages instead of 29. PDF sizes for the 1 / 5 / 30-page documents: PdfPecker 12 / 28 / 126 KB, Chromium 72 / 139 / 171 KB, wkhtmltopdf 30 / 59 / 191 KB, HtmlRenderer 35 / 65 / 273 KB, iText 26 / 45 / 104 KB, Syncfusion 42 / 89 / 132 KB. Each converter was used the way its documentation suggests for many documents: PdfPecker and HtmlRenderer in process, wkhtmltopdf as one process per document, and PuppeteerSharp and Playwright with one shared browser and a new tab per document (Playwright in one shared browser context, tagged PDF output off for both). iText reuses one font provider per thread, as its knowledge base advises. Syncfusion keeps one converter per concurrent conversion with ReuseBrowserProcess on, as its support forum advises, so the parallel run starts four browsers. IronPDF was not measured here. One user compared PdfPecker with IronPDF 2026.7.2 (Chrome-based) on the 26 templates of their production app, on a 22-core development machine after warm-up: IronPDF took 13.6 s for all 26 documents one at a time and PdfPecker 17 ms (about 800 times faster), and with 22 in parallel IronPDF made 9.2 documents/s and PdfPecker 1,143 (about 125 times). 24 of the 26 documents came out identical; the other two differ by less than 0.25 mm. To reproduce the table, clone the PdfPecker.Benchmarks repository (needs wkhtmltopdf on PATH and a Chromium at CHROMIUM_PATH) and run: dotnet run --project src/PdfPecker.Comparison -c Release It measures PdfPecker from nuget.org; -p:PdfPeckerVersion= picks another release. The comparison lives in its own repository, so its third-party packages never reach the library or its tests. Your numbers will differ with hardware and documents.

Measured with bench/PdfPecker.Benchmarks (in the PdfPecker repository) on a 4-core cloud VM (.NET 10, Release, after JIT warm-up): Document Pages Median Throughput Invoice with a PNG logo and a styled table 1 0.55 ms about 1,800 docs/s on one core Feature tour (text, lists, tables, JPEG and PNG) 5 2.5 ms about 1,700 docs/s on 4 cores Dense report with 1,000 table rows 30 19.5 ms about 1,500 pages/s on one core Markdown guide (guide.md, headings, lists, code, a table) to PDF 2 0.9 ms about 1,000 docs/s on one core Parsing Markdown to HTML runs at roughly 20 to 45 MB/s, so it is a small part of a Markdown to PDF conversion. The first conversion in a process also pays for JIT compilation; later ones run at the speeds above. About 80% of the first PDF's time is compiling PdfPecker's code, so an app that starts often (a command-line tool, a serverless function, a container that scales to zero) can publish with ReadyToRun to have it compiled ahead of time: dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishReadyToRun=true In a measured app this took the first PDF from about 345 ms to about 130 ms, while the published PdfPecker.dll grows from about 5 MB to about 10 MB, since it holds native code for one platform next to the IL. Later conversions run at the same speed either way. Native AOT, which PdfPecker supports too, removes the JIT entirely. Rendering PDF pages to images, same machine, one core per page (PdfRenderer, first render of each page of a freshly opened document, so fonts and images are decoded too): Document Render at 96 DPI Render at 150 DPI PNG encoding at 150 DPI Invoice (1 page) 13 ms 19 ms 24 ms Feature tour (5 pages) 7 ms per page 12 ms per page 26 ms per page Large report (30 pages) 5 ms per page 10 ms per page 29 ms per page Rendering the same page again (fonts and glyphs cached) takes about 5 ms at 150 DPI. Multi-page conversions render pages in parallel. Encoding one 150 DPI A4 page (1240 x 1754) takes about 15 to 60 ms as PNG, 20 to 70 ms as JPEG and 40 to 85 ms as WebP at the default quality, depending on content.

The source paths below are in the PdfPecker repository under src/PdfPecker/. Markdown is first turned into HTML: Markdown/BlockParser finds the block structure line by line, following the CommonMark reference algorithm, Markdown/InlineParser handles emphasis (delimiter stack) and links (bracket stack), and Markdown/HtmlRenderer writes the HTML, which then takes the same path as any other document: Html/HtmlParser builds a DOM in a single pass, applying the browser rules for implied end tags. Css/StyleResolver cascades a user-agent stylesheet, presentational attributes, document stylesheets and inline styles. Rules are indexed by id, class and tag, and elements with identical inputs share one computed style. For a tagged PDF, Pdf/StructureTree then maps the elements to structure types and gives every text node, image and list marker a slot in that tree. Layout/LayoutEngine lays out blocks, inline text (line breaking, justification), lists and tables (automatic column widths), paginating as it goes, and produces a flat list of draw operations. Inline content with right-to-left text gets its embedding levels from Text/Bidi (UAX #9), and each line is put in visual order after it is broken. Fonts/ComplexShaper shapes Arabic and Hebrew runs with the font's GSUB and GPOS tables (Fonts/OpenTypeLayout). Pdf/PdfDocumentWriter writes PDF 1.4: content streams, fonts, image XObjects, link annotations, the bookmark outline and the cross-reference table. A tagged PDF's content is wrapped in marked-content sequences for its slots (or as artifacts), and the structure tree and its parent tree are written last. Fonts/FontSubsetter and Fonts/CffSubsetter cut embedded fonts down to the glyphs used (with their composite components and the CFF subroutines they call). The renderer (Rendering/) works the other way round: Parsing/PdfFile reads the object graph, PageRenderer interprets content streams, Fonts/ turns glyphs into outlines (cached as anti-aliased bitmaps), Images/ decodes images, and Graphics/Rasterizer fills paths with exact area coverage before PngEncoder, JpegEncoder or WebPEncoder writes the result. The third-party fonts, font data and code built into the library are listed, with their licenses, in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.
